Section on the Compendium of Determinations (Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī), Part 1: The Stage Corresponding to the Five Groups of Consciousness and the Stage of Mind (13a–16a). 1.

Regarding the first part of the fifty-first section of the Main Treatise, the Section on the Compendium of Determinations, namely the Stage Corresponding to the Five Groups of Consciousness and the Stage of Mind: this...
This treatise consists of five parts in total.
The first fifty fascicles have already elucidated the essential meaning of the seventeen stages;
this constitutes the first part, the *Maulī Bhūmi* (Local Stages).
The latter four parts: their meanings are explained in detail below, as all preceding sections were titled "Inclusion" (*saṃgraha*).
This present section is the first among these latter four parts.
Because it is concise by means of summarizing what has not yet been definitively analyzed,
it is called the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* (Section on the Compendium of Definitive Analysis). Alternatively, some [call it so] because of its textual content.
The preceding section of the summary text is now restated as a distinct part.
Furthermore, according to the *Abhidharmakośa*, it is called the *Abhidharmapiṭaka* (Treasury of Abhidharma);
because the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*) is contained within that *Abhidharma* treatise, this work receives the name "Treasury" (*piṭaka*).
Alternatively, because this [basis] relies upon that, is drawn forth from it, and is stored within it, it is also called a "storehouse" (*ālaya*).
Since that [term] possesses these two meanings, this [term] is likewise so.
This is clarified by the fact that the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*) included in the *Maulī Bhūmi* is definitively determined within this section.

Alternatively, because this [section] relies on that [section], draws forth from its fundamental ground the very meanings contained therein, and is thus subsumed under that portion, it is called the "Section on the Determination of Subsumption" (Saṃgrahaviniścaya).
This, therefore, is a case of subsuming the text by means of the text.
Therefore, it is called "comprehension" (*saṃgraha*).
Alternatively, there are cases where the meaning is comprehended through the text;
although the first eight [sections] explain the essence of the Dharma, there are aspects of their meaning that remain unclarified.
Now, this is clarified as a single category:
just as it is said that the eye-element subsumes the eye-element, meaning that a self-nature subsumes itself;
or, in some cases, the meaning subsumes the text.
By means of this section, the essential points are determined and the incomplete passages from the preceding sections are condensed;
in some cases, meanings are subsumed under other meanings.
By means of the wisdom that definitively discerns what is expressed, one discriminates the differences between the various stages (*bhūmi*).
However, the meaning of this discrimination is uniform; thus, it is further subsumed [within the teaching], which is to say, this portion of the teaching is gathered by way of its meaning.
The designators that provide definitive discernment are named according to what they designate;
therefore, it is called "inclusion" (*saṃgraha*).
This clarifies the meaning of inclusion.
Thus, it comprises four propositions.
Regarding the term "decisive analysis" (*viniścaya*):
"decisive" (*vi*) refers to decisive resolution.
This means resolving the doubts of others;
it can also mean "to resolve" in the sense of "to fully comprehend," whereby one is able to understand for oneself.
"Discernment" (pravicaya) means to investigate thoroughly; it may be said to mean investigating what is right and what is wrong.
Here, this [text] clarifies what is correct and refutes what is incorrect.
Therefore, it is called "decisive determination" (*viniścaya*).
Although wrong views repudiate the ultimate and conventional truths, they do not involve the discernment of right from wrong;
although doubt involves the discernment of right from wrong, it lacks decisive resolution.
By means of decisive discourse, doubts and delusions are resolved;
by means of analytical discussion, heterodox views are distinguished.
In the preceding *Maulī Bhūmi*, the characteristics of the meanings were directly described.
Now, by means of repeated questions and answers, doubts are resolved and the essentials are selected;
therefore, it is named "Decisive Selection" (Viniścaya). The old translation as "Storehouse of Determination" (Niyata-piṭaka) is incorrect.
That which is called *vinaya* may be said to mean "definitive.
Since it is said that *vinaya* gives rise to *jñapti*,
this refers to "ascertainment" (*viniścaya*).
How can it be called "definitive"?
The treatise states that "parts" (bhāga) refers to "delimitations" (maryādā).
It is a section that distinguishes and classifies;
it is the intermediate portion following the "Local Ground" (*Maulī Bhūmi*) and preceding the "Explanatory Section" (*Vyākhyāna*). As for "middle": [it refers to this intermediate position].
The meaning of "selection and retention" (*saṃgraha*) is as follows: among the seventeen stages (*bhūmi*), fifteen other stages are excluded,
and these two specific stages are particularly elucidated.
Therefore, it is said that this is the middle [section].
As for the mention of the "Stage Associated with the Five Groups of Consciousness" and the "Stage of Mind," these have already been explained as recorded in the *Maulī Bhūmi*.
Question:
Why is it not called "mental consciousness" (manovijñāna)? Answer:
Because the name would be confused with other usages.
This clarifies the mind (citta), the intellect (manas), and consciousness (vijñāna); therefore, "consciousness" is not included [separately].
Question: Does the meaning of association (samprayoga) not apply exclusively to these five?
Why does the initial heading not mention that the mind exists?
Answer: In reality, they all exist;
it is merely omitted for the sake of brevity.
Furthermore, by mentioning the first, the subsequent is revealed;
therefore, the mental level (*manobhūmi*) is not explicitly stated as being associated.
Moreover, this is explained according to the preeminent dharmas.
The five consciousnesses lack grasping and so forth;
their objects are narrow and limited.
Since they are mentioned in association [with other factors], the sense organs and objects are not explicitly stated.
The *manas* consciousness also clarifies both [the seventh and eighth consciousnesses]; since the faculties, objects, and so forth of both the seventh and eighth consciousnesses are all clarified,
one cannot speak of "correspondence" (*samprayoga*) in a partial sense.
Therefore, it is omitted here.
Question: Since the preceding *Maulī Bhūmi* (Basic Section) has already been divided into two sections, why are they explained together here?
Answer: There are two reasons.
The six consciousnesses each have their own specific supports, namely the six sense organs (*ṣaḍindriya*),

while they share a common support, which is the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*). Here, we first clarify that the eighth consciousness is the common support for the five [sensory] and the sixth consciousness.
Therefore, they are combined for clarification.
The preceding section was distinguished as a separate stage based on meanings such as intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and functional activity (*karman*).
Second, the six consciousnesses are designated as the distinct seeds-supports (*bīja-āśraya*).
Although the *Maulī Bhūmi* clarifies the ālayavijñāna,
it does so only in terms of its function as the seeds-support.
This is explained in accordance with the six consciousnesses;
because their functions differ,
they are separately established as two distinct stages.
In this section, it is further clarified that the manifest eighth consciousness is the common support for the six consciousnesses.
Since it serves as a common support, it cannot be distinguished into two separate stages; the reason for this is that they are explained together.
Because it is taught from the eighth [consciousness], they are combined into one to clarify [this point].
Furthermore, this is discussed solely in terms of their functions; since their functions are distinct, [they must be separate].
It must be explained separately:
both rely on the sense faculties and take objects as their conditions;
their modes of activity and characteristics are identical.
Therefore, they are explained together.
Furthermore, as stated in the sixth fascicle of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*:
"Question: To which consciousness is the ālayavijñāna subsumed?"
Answer: It is subsumed within the six consciousnesses.
The previous [explanation] was a distinction based on seeds;
the present [explanation] is based on what is subsumed within the six consciousnesses.
Therefore, this section on the definitive analysis of the Grounds is compiled for clarity;
it consists of seven fascicles in total.
This is called "the first" because it is the very beginning;
within this section, there are thirty fascicles that resolve and determine the meaning of the preceding seventeen stages (*bhūmi*).
It is divided into twelve sections:
the five consciousness-bodies stage (*pañcavijñānakāyabhūmi*) and the mind stage (*manobhūmi*) are combined into one;
the stage with vitarka and vicāra, etc. (*savitarkasavicārādibhūmi*) is another.
The stages of the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha constitute one;
this is because the stage with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa*) and the stage without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa*) are combined into one.
That is to say, the first seven fascicles combine and resolve the *Pañcavijñānakāyabhūmi*.
The *Manobhūmi*.
Next, four fascicles resolve the three stages beginning with "With Vitarka" (*savitarkādi*).
Next, one and a half fascicles resolve the *Samāhitabhūmi*.
Next, the one leaf and more of the sixty-third [fascicle] definitely belong to the *Samāhitā-bhūmi*.
Next, the two leaves and more definitely belong to the *Sacittikā-bhūmi*.
Next, the two and a half leaves definitely belong to the *Acittikā-bhūmi*.
Next, scroll sixty-four resolves the stage of wisdom derived from hearing;
the next two scrolls resolve the stage of wisdom derived from reflection;
and next, approximately three pages within scroll sixty-seven resolve the stage of wisdom derived from cultivation.
From the end of the sixty-seventh fascicle through four and a half fascicles,
the *Śrāvakabhūmi* and *Pratyekabuddhabhūmi* are combined and resolved; however,
the title refers only to the *Śrāvakabhūmi* and does not resolve the *Pratyekabuddhabhūmi*.
From the seventieth fascicle down to the middle of the eightieth, these eight and a half fascicles together constitute the definitive exposition of the Bodhisattvabhūmi.
Next, the latter half of the eightieth fascicle constitutes the combined definitive exposition of the Sopadhiśeṣa-nirupadhiśeṣa-bhūmi.
This fundamental determination corresponds to four propositions.
First: union at the beginning and separation at the end;
this refers to the stage of having mind and the stage of no-mind-ground.
Second, separation at the beginning and conjunction at the end;
this refers to the simultaneous arising of the five bodies of consciousness and the mental ground, inquiring about the stage of the Pratyekabuddha and the stage with remainder.
Third, conjunction at both the beginning and the end.
This refers to the three stages beginning with "with vitarka" (savitarka).

The four [stages] that are free from both the initial and subsequent [vitarka and vicāra] refer to the remaining six stages: namely, the stage of meditative equipoise (samāhita-bhūmi), the stage not in meditative equipoise (asamāhita-bhūmi), the stage consisting of what is produced through hearing, reflection, and cultivation (śruta-cintā-bhāvanā-maya-bhūmi), and the Bodhisattva stage.
Within the first section, the initial part provides a general exposition of the benefits by concluding the preceding and introducing the subsequent;
the latter part provides a formal exposition based on the stages (*bhūmi*).
Although the initial passage is general and brief,
it is presented first within the five consciousnesses and the mental ground (*manobhūmi*).
Regarding the formal analysis, there are three parts.
First, the two grounds are briefly distinguished and explained individually;
next, they are correctly analyzed through questions and answers;
finally, their summary and definitive resolution are concluded.
Within the section on the correct determination through question and answer,
there is first a specific decision and resolution,
followed by a general analysis.
The preceding section consists of two parts. First,
from the beginning up to the latter half of the third fascicle, there is a brief explanation of the six kinds of skillfulness.
The second [section], from the latter half of the third fascicle onwards, extensively explains the six kinds of skillfulness (*ṣaḍkauśalya*).
Within this, there are ten gates; the first is the gate of mind, consciousness, and awareness (*citta-vijñāna-manas*).
Second, the discernment of the thorough knowledge of the body;
third, the discernment of the distinctions between the two types of skillfulness;
fourth, the determination of the causes and conditions through the reasoning of proof.
Five, explaining the meaning of formations dissociated from consciousness;
six, clarifying their seeds;
seven, interpreting karma.
18. Explaining the two mindless attainments (*acittaka-samāpatti*).
9. Explaining space (*ākāśa*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
10. A general exposition of the names and meanings of the dissociated factors (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*).
Within the first section, there are three parts:
first, the definitive determination of the meanings of *citta*, *manas*, and *vijñāna*;
second, the fourfold logical analysis (*catuṣkoṭi*) regarding their possession (*samanvāgama*).
The third section consists of questions and answers for clarification.
Within this, there are three parts:
first, restating what has already been explained and raising three questions.
Next follows the correct answer based on the question,
followed by the conclusion.
Within the question, there are again three parts.
First, the preceding foundational consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) is cited as the subject to be determined.
Second, three introductory questions are opened to establish the basis for inquiry.
Third, the three questions are formally posed to initiate the definitive analysis.
Question: Regarding the previous statement that the support for seeds is the *ālayavijñāna*, this refers to the first [point].
That is to say, it has already been clarified in the preceding *Maulī Bhūmiḥ* (Local Division) that the eighth consciousness is the support for all seeds.
Since seeds all depend upon existence (*bhava*),
yet the meaning of the extensive analysis of the causes and conditions for that existence has not been explained,
this constitutes the second opening of three questions as the basis for inquiry.
As for the statement that it has not yet been taught that [the eighth consciousness] exists: although the aforementioned *Maulī Bhūmi* extensively teaches that the eighth [consciousness] exists,
it has not yet been taught in the sūtras of the Hīnayāna.
This is the first question.
As the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* cites from a Hīnayāna sūtra, saying: "One loves, delights in, rejoices in, practices, and becomes attached to the ālayavijñāna.
The sūtras with which [this treatise] accords also speak in this same way.
If this statement already exists within the sūtras of the Hīnayāna, for what reason is it said that it does not yet exist?
Jñānagarbha sets forth two interpretations regarding why it is considered non-existent. First: [it is non-existent] because...
The Sarvāstivādins and others explain it thus;
furthermore, although that sūtra speaks of its existence,
its substance is precisely the sixth [consciousness].
There is no separate referent nor any other distinct meaning, such as the detailed analysis of causes and conditions;
that which does not yet exist has no separate substantial existence,
for it is not an existence by way of name.
Regarding the conditions for existence:
this is the reason why there is an eighth [link]. Although it is said that existence exists, [it does so] through these conditions.
The reason for the existence [of the latent dispositions] was previously unknown; now that the reason for their existence is known, the eighth [category] is maintained.
Its detailed analysis of the meaning of its simultaneous occurrence with the manifest factors, such as feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth, follows.
This constitutes the third question.
From the phrase "Why is it not stated...
onwards, the third section formally sets forth three questions to bring about definitive discernment (*viniścaya*).
As for why it is not mentioned:
it is simply because the question concerns a slight difference;
the rest of the text is self-evident.

Master Jing said: In the preceding "Local Basis" (*mūla-sthāna*) section, within the analysis of the five consciousnesses and the mental ground (*manobhūmi*), it is stated that there are five questions beginning with "What is the self-nature?
and so forth, establishing that the supports (*āśraya*) of consciousness are fourfold.
First, the basis of life, which refers to the seed-consciousness;
second, the defiled basis, which refers to the manas-consciousness;
third, the basis of birth, which refers to the five sense organs.
The fourth stage is the cessation of the mental faculty (*manas*), which refers to the mutual production of the six consciousnesses;
this shall now be explained through question and answer.
The sense of "the basis from which seeds arise" is precisely the meaning of the discriminating mind (*vikalpa-citta*).
Since the ālayavijñāna is the mind (*citta*), the manas is the intellect (*manas*), and the six consciousnesses are the cognitions (*vijñāna*),
according to the underlying principle, this section refers specifically to the discriminating mind alone;
however, in the concluding summary below, it comprehensively encompasses all three— mind, intellect, and cognition.
"By this, it is established that he is the Buddha, the World-Honored One"—
this is the second answer.
Within the response, three answers are given in accordance with the questions.
This answers the first question.
That is to say, the ālayavijñāna is subtle;
bodhisattvas prior to the stages (bhūmi) produce understanding in accordance with the teachings, yet they are not yet able to fully comprehend it.
Therefore, no distinction is made regarding the two vehicles;
thus it is said that the reason for not speaking [of them] was recorded in secret.
This is as the World-Honored One stated below:
Citing the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*,
it correctly explains that [the Buddha] did not speak [of this].
The first phrase reveals the general profundity and subtlety.
The second and fourth phrases explicitly clarify the reason why [the Buddha] did not speak;
the third phrase explicitly clarifies that he did not speak.
Question: Why do the fourth and second phrases clarify the reason for not speaking?
The answer is that it is not mentioned for two reasons.
First, it is not mentioned because it is profound and subtle;
this refers to the second point, which correctly clarifies the meaning of its profundity and subtlety.
The second [category] consists of those for whom he does not teach out of fear that afflictions might arise;
this corresponds to the fourth case.
As for the statement, "The ādānavijñāna is profound and subtle":
Jingyun said:
"For Bodhisattvas prior to the stage of the ground (*bhūmi*), it is called 'profound' because they have not yet fully understood it;
for those of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*), it is called 'subtle' because they do not penetrate it."
Master Ji’s statement that both the seventh and eighth consciousnesses are called *ādāna* in the older translations is incorrect.
As the verse in the older treatise states:
"The appropriating consciousness (*ādānavijñāna*) is profound and subtle."
Since it is said that the seventh [consciousness] "grasps and maintains," how could it possibly maintain [anything else]?
In Sanskrit it is called *kliṣṭa-manas*,
which here means "defiled mind."
Now, as for what is called *ādāna*, it refers to the eighth [consciousness] in the sense of "grasping" or "maintaining. Question:
In the older treatises, the grasping consciousness is described as profound and subtle.
"What is the difference now?
[The respondent] said: "The term 'upādāna' (grasping/holding) is correct in its meaning."
However, there is a distinct meaning in this "exclusion" (*pratiṣedha*) that differs from other exclusions. Why is this so?
It is because the previous mention of being "profound and subtle" excluded only ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*), but did not exclude the followers of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*).
The meanings relied upon by ordinary worldlings are all coarse and shallow;
this [teaching] is profound and subtle, and thus merely distinguishes itself from the worldlings.
As for the teachings of the two vehicles, they are all likewise profound and subtle, so this [teaching] should be equal to them.
Therefore, it is now distinguished from the two vehicles by means of extreme brevity;
for the scriptures and teachings of the two vehicles are profound and subtle, and thus not "extreme.
Since this [teaching] is complete, it must be distinct.
Therefore, it is stated below that only noble ones who have realized the truths (*satyadarśin*) are able to fully understand this, while others cannot;
prior to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the sixth consciousness, when performing the contemplation of representation-only (*vijñaptimātratā*), has not yet perceived the eighth consciousness.
One comes to know this only upon entering into [the realization of] the view;
therefore, it is said to be "profound and subtle. Ce (測) states that the name *ādāna* is explained through three meanings:
first, it is called "grasping" (*ādāna*) by virtue of its function of holding fast (*dhṛti*).
First, it is called "retention" because it can maintain the seeds of names, marks, and so forth, preventing them from being lost. Second,
it is called "appropriation" because it can appropriate the physical sense organs and their bases, enabling the arising of sensation and perception.
Third is grasping by way of attachment,
which refers to the capacity to grasp and maintain the continuity of rebirth;
sentient beings lacking such a nature cannot fathom its depths.
Therefore, it is said to be profound.
Because those of the lineage who incline toward tranquility cannot penetrate it,
it is called profound.
This is as explained in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
If one follows Vasubandhu, it should be interpreted by combining these two [texts] deeply and subtly.
Therefore, that treatise states:
"That which is profound and subtle is difficult to comprehend."
Yet it is not assigned a clan name.
If one follows Asvabhāva,
that which is called "profound" is as follows:
Because the wisdom awakened by those of worldly brilliance has a bottomless depth,
it is said to be "extremely subtle," as it is difficult for śrāvakas and others to comprehend.
Now, upon examining the old translations,
they differ from the phrasing of the current text.
As it says in the *Laghumati-bodhisattva-manas-karma-śāstra*:
In the profound *Saṃdhinirmocana Mahāyāna Sūtra*, the Blessed One spoke of the appropriating consciousness (*ādānavijñāna*),
which is subtle, difficult to measure,
and possesses immeasurable seeds.
Their number is like raindrops;
I do not preach this Dharma to ordinary persons.
It is not because of a desire for it;
rather, one fears further conceptualization of a self.
"All seeds are like a violent torrent" means:
This single phrase cites the profound and subtle nature of the eighth consciousness but does not explain it;
this is precisely the reason why the first [point], "profound and subtle," is not explained.
Master Jing said:
Regarding the statement in the *Aṅgula* that the ādāna-vijñāna is the tathāgatagarbha:
because the ālaya-vijñāna contains the seeds of the afflictions,
it is able to conceal that dharmakāya of the Tathāgata, and is thus named the tathāgatagarbha.
Furthermore, within the ālayavijñāna there exist the undefiled seeds of that Tathāgata which can store manifold fruits; this is called the *tathāgatagarbha*.
Moreover, it is said that there are nine or eight kinds of consciousnesses.
Taken collectively among the various consciousnesses,
there are nine grades of discernment;
it is not intended here to debate whether consciousness consists of eight or nine types.
Master Ji said: "When water has not yet been struck by wind, it is called 'still flow';
only when encountering wind and waves does it form rising billows.
This consciousness is likewise."
When the wind that can perfume has not yet stirred,
there is merely a continuous, level flow from moment to moment.
However, when the wind that can perfume does stir, [the waves arise].
The seeds become manifest like waves; or,
the seeds give rise to the manifest,
just as waves arise.
When the cause for one wave arrives, one wave arises;
when the causes for many waves arrive, many waves arise.
Question: Previously, it was stated that the transformation of seeds is like a constant flow;
how does this differ from the present case? Response: Although they are called "seeds," [the nature of their transformation differs].
It is not necessarily so; the previous statement may be considered restrictive.
The present statement, however, encompasses all meanings.
Furthermore, as for the expression "constant flow," what is its meaning?
If it refers to a flow like that of the Ganges River, then it is not so;
for how could a flow that is constant [in nature] be explained in terms of the meaning of causal perfuming (*hetu-vāsanā*)?
The meaning of "flood" (ogha) spoken of now lies herein.
Regarding the phrase, "I do not reveal this to the foolish and ignorant," this single sentence correctly clarifies the third point: that [the teaching] was not expounded.
Jingyun: I have previously explained in the *Ekottarika Āgama* that these are collectively termed "delight," "pleasure," "craving," "habituation," and "attachment.
I fear that [further elaboration] would increase the dualistic grasping at persons and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-grāha*).
Yet he did not explain it to them in detail. [The interlocutor] asks:
Does the Buddha not teach the *ālayavijñāna* to those of the two vehicles?
For those of the two vehicles do not give rise to the view of a self.
Furthermore, the ālayavijñāna is not taught to ordinary beings (pṛthagjana).
[If it were,] ordinary beings would have no conceptual view of a self.
Answer: Although ordinary beings lack a conceptual view of a self arising based on the Buddha’s teachings, [they still possess it].
However, based on those heterodox and false teachings, there arises the conceptualization of a self.
Jizang states that while this exists nominally in the Hīnayāna,
it lacks substantial reality.
I do not expound this to the ignorant,
for it is merely a name;
even the names used by ordinary worldlings have not yet reached it.
This refers to my not explaining [the truth] to ordinary people.
If, according to the Hīnayāna, it is called "already possessed," I do not expound upon it;
if it is called "not yet possessed," I likewise do not explain it.
Question: Since [the Dharma] was not expounded for the sake of those of the two vehicles or ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), why is it now being taught so that ordinary beings may hear it?
Answer: Within this, there are both types of persons.
Among the śrāvakas, there are two types of persons:
first, those whose faculties are not yet mature; second, those whose faculties are not fully matured.
Because they are either of a definite nature or of an indefinite nature, [the Buddha] does not provide an exposition for them.
If they are of an indefinite nature and their faculties have matured,
why does he not provide an exposition for them?
Ordinary beings are likewise:
first, those who lack the spiritual lineage because one faculty is immature;
second, those whose faculties are not yet matured.
Therefore, it was not taught to them.
Now, as for those who hear it,
they have all attained it because their faculties were already matured.
The statement that "it is not disclosed to the foolish and ignorant" has its meaning in this very point. Question:
Previously, it was said, "I do not speak of this to the foolish."
"What is the difference between these?
Shu replied, "They are indeed not different.
It is simply that [the former] excludes ordinary beings but does not exclude those of the two vehicles."
Therefore, my intention in speaking now is this:
I fear that those who conceptually construct and cling to [the self] as being the "self" refer precisely to the fourth alternative.
The second [point] explains why it is not stated that afflictions arise;
for ordinary beings have not yet severed the two attachments,
and there is a fear that the attachment to the two selves might arise.
Although the person-self (*pudgala-ātman*) has been eliminated for those of the two vehicles, the dharma-self (*dharma-ātman*) still remains;
fearing that they might give rise to this [view],
I speak of two kinds of self.
First, the discriminating [self];
second, the co-emergent [self].
The co-emergent self arises spontaneously.
The conceptualized self arises only through teaching;
for fear that ordinary beings might give rise to a conceptualization of two selves based on the teaching,
and that those of the Two Vehicles might give rise to a conceptualization of the self of phenomena (*dharma-ātman*) based on causes and conditions.
Therefore, it was not taught for them.
Question: Previously it was said that they should not grasp [the aggregates] as a self; how does this differ?
The commentary states: This statement generally does not yet distinguish the "self" that arises spontaneously (*anābhoga*); its meaning can be understood accordingly.
Question: The eighth consciousness-continuum appears to be unitary and permanent;
one fears that this might give rise to the view of a personal self (*pudgala-dṛṣṭi*), which ordinary people have never heard of.
The fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) possesses a substantial nature and is real;
however, it is not mentioned here because its grasping at dharmas (dharmagrāha) is so great.
The commentary states that although that eighth consciousness gives rise to the grasping at dharmas, [it is not discussed for this reason].
If one wishes to eliminate the attachment to phenomena, it must be through Consciousness-Only (Vijñaptimātra).
Since the eighth consciousness is the causal condition for all phenomena as they truly are,
it is the very foundation of Consciousness-Only.
Therefore, for those of great faculties, it is taught that the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) exists, and so forth.
Regarding the meaning of this consciousness:
when the Buddha expounds the Dharma, he takes the benefit of sentient beings as its primary purpose.
If one were to say that this dharma, at its beginning, does not fall into birth and death, and at its end, enables the attainment of nirvana, the Buddha would indeed speak thus;
yet when ordinary people hear of this consciousness, they give rise to the dualistic discrimination of two selves.

that which is "mine" should likewise be so.
Therefore, it is not a latent tendency (anuśaya) conditioned by another realm.

Question: When the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) takes form and other objects of the higher realms as its object, why is it said that it immediately follows the seeing-portion (darśana-bhāga) bound to the desire realm?

If the eighth [consciousness] takes the formal characteristics (*nimitta-rūpa*) and so forth of the higher realms as its objects, it would consequently be bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-saṃprayukta*).
To this, we reply: it is not so.
This is because the eighth [consciousness] contains the seeds, and those seeds pertain to all realms.
The sixth case is not so;
therefore, it cannot serve as an analogy.
Because there is a transformation of seeds related to [the realm], the object of the eighth [consciousness] is not bound to the desire realm.
The sixth consciousness and others are called "seed-image conditions" (*bīja-bimba-pratyaya*); therefore, they follow the realm of attachment (*dhātu-bandhana*) of the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*).
Furthermore, it is explained that when Dharmapāla [the seventh consciousness] takes the eighth [consciousness] as its object, there is no sense of "mine" (*mamakāra*).
It is said that they do not exist there because this is a general statement.
Regarding the five sense organs transformed by the three fundamental consciousnesses,
now only those transformed by one's own [consciousness] remain, as the actual karma has ceased.
It is not the other two kinds of five sense-faculties.

When this [consciousness] takes the internal as its object, the four great elements that produce sound exist at all times; thus, by way of conventional designation, the element of sound is said to exist.
In reality, it does not exist;
rather, it is named "conditioned by sound" because it arises from the seeds of sound and the four great elements.
It is not the case that manifest sound exists at all times.
In this context, there must be a time when one great element increases, such as the earth element within the eye;
at that time, the body faculty, the eye, and the four objects—these seven entities—can be perceived, whereas the others cannot be perceived.
When those increase, they are also said to be conditions.
Their protection consists solely of two kinds of five faculties,
which are transformations of the eighth and sixth consciousnesses.
The seventh [consciousness] takes only the eighth as its object,
regarding it as "I" and "mine. Regarding this,
Ratnacandra challenges the doctrine, saying:
If the upper [realms] do not take the lower external vessel-world as an object,
for what reason does the eighth consciousness arise as the divine eye?
Furthermore, it is said that this is not the object of the eighth consciousness.
Therefore, it does not take [an object] as its condition; it is solely that which is traversed by the mind.
If this is so, then where there is no object, there is no mind.
The mind does not take this as its object;
the eighth consciousness does not take it as its object either;
therefore, the eye should not exist.
If that were so, just as the five consciousnesses are not the objects of the eighth [consciousness] and the manas does not take them as its object,
would these five consciousnesses then simply not exist?
Consciousness is that which is grasped by the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) with respect to its objective support (*ālambana*).
This eye is not the seeing-part (darśana-bhāga); how then can it serve as an example?
It also functions as the seeing-part in accordance with consciousness; therefore, it is the same as the five sensory consciousnesses.
The commentary states:
It is not necessarily the case that [an object] must be destroyed by karma to serve as an object-condition;
for example, the eighth [consciousness] also takes as its object things such as the nourished faculties (*upacita-indriya*) of the lower realms.
Just as a seed, though not produced by karma,
is nonetheless not prevented from serving as a condition for the eighth consciousness;
if that is so, why do you not allow that the external receptacle world may also serve as an object-condition when one is born into a higher realm from a lower one?
The following is the eighth [point], because it takes the eye of the upper realms as its object;
this will be explained in detail below.
This pertains to the realms that possess form (rūpadhātu) and so forth.
Bei said: "This passage follows the interpretation of Dharmapāla.
For if it were another's body, it would lack appropriation (anupātta)."
Master Ji, recounting Dharmapāla’s position, said:

"If the eighth [consciousness] of the formless realm does not take the lower receptacle world as its object, why does the text concerning the external receptacle world preemptively specify: 'This [occurs] within the realm of form'?"
Therefore, it is known that the formless realm takes the external receptacle world of the lower realms as its object.
Dharmapāla says: "This is a textual clarification regarding internal grasping."
If there is the realm of form (rūpadhātu), there are seeds, faculties (indriya), and the bases of the faculties;
in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), there are only seeds, but no faculties nor the sensory objects that support them.
Thus, regarding internal appropriation, it is half-existent and half-non-existent, and must be distinguished from matter (rūpa).
Within external appropriated [objects], everything belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) is absent;
why, then, is it necessary to make such a distinction?
Therefore, there is the analogy of the wick and the oil below.

If there were external receptacle worlds in the formless realm, they would lack internal wicks; since there is light externally, it is known that [the analogy] is distinguished [from the case at hand].
Thus, it does not accord with your intention.

Regarding the eighth category— those transformed by the five types of consciousness that are associated with the number of sentient beings, such as the bodies of others, which are both sentient and non-sentient— they are indeed of the number of sentient beings. If this is so,
why are they not considered maturation (*vipāka*)?
It is said that the faculties (*indriya*) are the supports for consciousness.
This is also true;
however, this is not yet based on their fundamental origination.
Regarding the phrase "discerning the appearance of the external,
non-conceptual vessel" and "up to the appearances of the vessel-world," the Supplement states:
The ālayavijñāna internally maintains the seeds of both internal and external common characteristics, from which the external world arises without interruption;
thus, it is established based upon both the internal and the external.
Now follows the second question.
It simply refers to the external receptacle world that is produced; therefore,
it is said that "the capacity" extends even to the characteristics of the receptacle world,
which is the common seed capable of producing it.
The previous questions have been concluded.
For example, even down to that which emits external light, the flame is a metaphor for the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*),
and the wick and oil are metaphors for the seeds of common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇabīja*).
The emission of external radiance that fills all locations is a metaphor for the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*).
Tai [Zongyi] says:
"Discriminating" refers to the *ālaya-vijñāna* being able to discriminate the characteristics of the external receptacle world.
Regarding the phrase "the basis for the cognition of internal [objects] and so forth" in the *Vyākhyāyukti*:

it means that one portion of the *ālayavijñāna* takes internal grasping (*upādāna*) and seeds as its object, while another portion discriminates the appearances of the external vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*).

Within a portion of the external receptacle world, the ālayavijñāna—which takes as its support that consciousness which discerns the internal seeds—externally transforms into the appearance of the external receptacle world;
this occurs constantly and without interruption.
The arising of the lamp flame is a metaphor for the external vessel-world that possesses discernment;
the oil is like the appropriated seeds;
and the wick is a metaphor for the ālayavijñāna.
The "light" is a metaphor for the external vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*). This refers to the manifestation of the external vessel-world based upon its seeds and based upon the *ālayavijñāna*;
it does not separately explain the agent that performs this discernment.

Regarding the phrase "the undifferentiated characteristic of the receptacle world," one interpretation states that because the external receptacle world transformed by the ālayavijñāna of all sentient beings is, at one time and in one place, without distinction of characteristics and constitutes a single vessel.
It is called "non-conceptual.
Furthermore, it is explained that through the power of common karma within the ālayavijñāna, a single wind is induced at the place of residence;
because there is no sense of enjoyment in other worlds, [it is non-conceptual].
The manifested appearance of the receptacle world is without interruption;
therefore, it is called "non-conceptual.
It may also be so called because it is not a sentient being.

It is called "non-conceptual" because its faculties, objects, and so forth are not conceptually differentiated; yet it is called "conceptual" because it is subsumed under the category of sentient beings.
Furthermore, regarding the statement that "the ālayavijñāna’s perception of objects is so subtle that even those of worldly wisdom find it difficult to comprehend," Jing says:
"The ālayavijñāna currently manifests as the cognition of the self-characteristics (svalakṣaṇa) of phenomena."
Just as visual consciousness perceives a forest as a whole, so too does the ālayavijñāna;
in a single moment, the visual consciousness produces a differentiated understanding that knows the specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa) of phenomena.
The same applies to the ālayavijñāna.
In a single thought-moment, one suddenly knows the infinite hundreds of thousands of distinctions between the internal body and the external vessel-world;
to discern these prior matters through distinct practice and understanding is called "knowing their specific characteristics" (svalakṣaṇa),
and this is termed "simultaneous measurement."
Therefore, one should know that within each and every moment of the ālayavijñāna, many modes of activity and understanding arise;
since these activities and understandings are numerous and their cognitive objects are subtle,
even those of worldly wisdom and intelligence cannot comprehend them.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "from the ālayavijñāna up to the transformation as the discernment of a single flavor," Jì (基) states:
"In this context,
Dharmapāla’s [commentary] serves as the primary text."
Śīlabhadra said: "If one takes the environment of the three realms as an object,
why is it stated here only that [the ālayavijñāna] persists from the initial appropriation until the end of life?"
The Master replied:
"This is merely explained by taking a single internal body as the basis for discussing the external vessel-world;
it does not accord with the ultimate meaning."
Question: Just as karma in this realm ceases and returns to this same realm—
like the death and rebirth in a higher realm occurring when the karma of that very realm is exhausted— so too does birth [occur].
If it has not been exhausted, how can one be born in a higher realm?
If it has been exhausted, for what reason is one still born in a higher realm while taking the external vessel-world of the lower realm as an object?
Furthermore, if one is born in a higher realm, why would one still take that external vessel-world as an object?
Furthermore, the physical world (*bhājana-loka*) would never come to an end.
To explain: this refers to the bodies of sentient beings and their distinct external objects of enjoyment.
When karma is exhausted, its fruit is exhausted.
While there is karma, there are external conditions that produce distinct fruits;
however, those common external environmental fruits do not necessarily require karma.
First, there is the condition of expedient means (*upāya-pratyaya*), because at all times it spontaneously takes that as its object.
Question: If that is so, then...
As stated in various treatises, although the external vessel-world of the fourth dhyāna is not destroyed by the three calamities, it arises and perishes along with the bodies [of its inhabitants].
Since this vessel-world that arises and perishes along with them is a fruit of common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa-phala*), how is it that it perishes?
Because they spontaneously take [those objects] as their object at all times;
although this should likewise be the case for the earth-elements of the lower realms,
it is not explained in the treatises concerning the four dhyānas.
The commentary says:
This statement is made based on the most eminent conditions. What is its meaning?
First, there are the conditions such as dwellings and houses, which are experienced by sentient beings individually;
whereas the external receptacle world is experienced collectively by sentient beings,
even though it is summoned by a common karma.
However, the karmic force of this particular sentient being increases because they possess distinct superior conditions for experience;
as long as these superior conditions remain present, [the result will continue].
Other sentient beings may undergo transformation accordingly;
if there is no superior condition, they will experience this very place as well.
Question: If that is so, what if one sentient being is also a common object of perception for other sentient beings?
Furthermore, it is spoken of as being experienced in accordance with predominant conditions;
since both the sentient beings and those predominant conditions already exist,
the sentient beings should likewise take them as their objects.
Since this principle is difficult to refute,
it cannot be accepted.
Furthermore, it is as if hell must be summoned by evil karma.
If one is born among humans or devas, by what karma is this induced?
If those in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) can also take it as an object,
why is it that the body in the form realm still gives rise to various unwholesome karmas of the hells that are able to induce their results?
Therefore, there is a great contradiction.
As for the question of how this principle applies to the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla,
the explanation is as follows:
If those in the upper realms do not take the lower realms as an object,
there is no logical contradiction;
however, at what time do humans and devas of the desire realm create karma for those [upper realms]?
If this is karma induced by humans or devas,
it must be a wholesome induction,
for humans and devas do not undergo birth there.
If one has already been destined for rebirth by the retribution of evil karma, and further adds other evil karmas,
there is no contradiction in this case;
it is like perceiving excrement and imagining it to be delicious food.
The principle is thus. Furthermore,
if the eighth consciousness did not take the form and other objects of the higher realms as its objects,
then how could this eye-faculty— which functions like the supernormal power of the divine eye— be an object of the eighth consciousness?
Answer: It does not take [external objects] as its object-condition.
If that is so, how can it be called "consciousness-only"?
Answer: It is called "consciousness-only" (vijñapti-mātra) because it arises from seeds, not because it is the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) of consciousness.
This refers to the sixth and seventh consciousness-elements acting as conditions and so forth.
Furthermore, it is said: "If that is the case, why do you not allow [the mind] to take the higher realms as its object?
The meaning is as follows:
If one goes to that realm,
for what reason are the forms bound to the form realm not guarded by [the restraint of] non-informative matter?
It is not the eighth condition,
because the objects seen and their respective fetters are distinct;
it is in reference to that [eighth condition] that the question is posed.
Because one transforms oneself into a reflected image,
as in the case of the bhikṣu Aśvajit;
entering pure lands and so forth, one goes everywhere according to one's will, transforming immediately upon whatever is seen.
It belongs to the category of being bound by views;
however, that which pertains to the realm of form (rūpadhātu) is bound by form and takes it as its object.
Regarding the statement that within the desire realm one takes as objects of perception narrow and limited appropriated entities (*upātta-viṣaya*) and so forth, Tai says:
"Narrow and limited" and "vast and great" do not refer solely to the body, but also include seeds as objects of appropriation.
Because these [seeds] are both the narrow and broad causes and also the fruits thereof.
Question: Since the seeds of the eighth and seventh consciousnesses are neither narrow nor broad causes and fruits, are they included herein?
Answer: As stated in the treatise, the mind of the desire realm is called "small mind," while the minds of the form realm and above are called "great mind.
Since they are the seeds of small and great minds, they are also termed "narrow" and "vast," and so forth.
Master Bei said:
"This text also accords with the meaning of Dharmapāla.
If one follows Śrīlāta,"
It should be said that the ālayavijñāna of the desire realm takes five kinds of objects as its conditions,
and so on up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, which likewise takes all five objects as its conditions;
thus, the Supplement (Pū-k’uei) states:
This passage clarifies that [the mind] takes the internal body as its object,
for the text consistently states that it takes the appropriated (*upātta*) as its object.
The body of the desire realm is narrow and small, whereas the body of the form realm is vast and extensive.
In the stages above the Sphere of Infinite Space and the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness,

the ālayavijñāna takes only seeds as its object; yet it is said that these two spheres take as their objects the immeasurable realms of appropriation because the seeds are perfumed by the practice of the contemplation of the pervasive pervasiveness of space and consciousness.
Because the ālayavijñāna takes that pervasive observation as its object, it is called "taking the immeasurable as its object.
From the pervasive observation of the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*),
even if one further investigates, nothing— neither form nor non-form— can be found apart from consciousness.
Consequently, the understanding of non-existence arises and perfumes [the mind] to form seeds;
at that stage, the ālayavijñāna takes those seeds as its object, which is termed "taking a subtlely grasped object.
The mental formations of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception are the most subtle, and they perfume [the mind] to form seeds.
Therefore, when that ālayavijñāna takes as its object the seeds of its own level,
it is said to take as its object the extremely subtle *upādāna* (appropriated) realm.
How is the extent of a single desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) within the external vessel-world to be known?
How should one understand the extent of a single realm of form (*rūpadhātu*)?
The Tripiṭaka Master says:
"The measure of the fourth dhyāna, when projected downward to cover [the lower realms], constitutes the extent of one desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and one realm of form."
Just as the first dhyāna covers a small chiliocosm—
wherein there is one Brahmā king over a thousand sets of four continents—
the second dhyāna covers a medium chiliocosm.
It covers a thousand Brahmā-worlds;
the third dhyāna covers a great trichiliocosm,
which is to say, it covers a million Brahmā-worlds.
The fourth dhyāna covers immeasurable realms;
that is, it covers the realms of immeasurable Brahmā kings.
Therefore, based on all the domains of the fourth meditative absorption (dhyāna), the extent covered below constitutes one form realm (rūpadhātu) and one desire realm (kāmadhātu).
Regarding the term "immeasurable" (apramāṇa):
it is called immeasurable because it is contrasted with the broad third dhyāna.
Thus, it is termed "immeasurable."
It is not said that they are "immeasurable" because they transcend all numbers;
rather, it is because through the ten directions of dhyāna, immeasurable triple-world systems (triloka) come to exist.
Therefore, there are many triple-world systems extending both horizontally and vertically.
Master Ji said:
"This is discussed in terms of the body;
because the dimensions of the body are small, it is called 'narrow and small'."
There is another interpretation: it is spoken of in terms of the external dimensions of the vessel-world,
such as the Small Thousandfold World and so forth.
Master Ji further states that the eighteen elements (*dhātu*) are designated as "small" or "large" based on their relative extent.
For instance, since those in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) lack both form and body, by what standard could they be considered small or large?
Therefore, he says that the various elements are named "small" or "large" [in relation to one another].
The meaning of how the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) is described in terms of the magnitude of its *dharmāyatana* has not yet been understood.
The Tripitaka Master said:
When that mind is perfumed— whether extensively or concisely— to form seeds,
the eighth consciousness takes these seeds as its object;
because the seeds arise from actual manifestations, they are termed "extensive" or "concise," but [the eighth consciousness] does not take the actual manifestations themselves as its object.
If that were so, one could say that the eighth consciousness takes as its object the seeds of the three realms.
Answer: Not so. This is based on their functional capacity, just as the desire realm is termed "narrow and small" (parīttābhāḥ).
Because the manifest activities produced by those seeds are likewise limited;
this applies even up to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
This is provided that, in the case of the desire and form realms, the external vessel-world (*bhājanaloka*) is not being discussed.
Because both take as their object the immeasurable external vessel-world (*bhājanaloka*), the second [section] clarifies the characteristic of evolving in association.
It says: "The eight [consciousnesses] are accompanied by five factors."
Master Ji said:
"This is the perfumer; this is the perfumed.
The commentary states:
It is not that the King lacks power such that he cannot correspond with the perfumer;
rather, it is that he is not the perfumed,
because he lacks the capacity [to be so].
Because it is not produced by the impulse of a preparatory mind (*prayoga-citta*),
it is not an impregnating agent (*vāsaka*). Now,
as for that which is an impregnating agent:
Only that which is produced by being drawn forth from a preceding preparatory mind can constitute a perfuming agent;
therefore, these five dharmas cannot be perfuming agents.
If that is so, then among the six consciousnesses, the neutral feeling of maturation (vipāka-upekṣā)—
It should be understood that these are likewise neither the perfumer nor the object of perfuming.
The Master says: "This is so, and there is no fault."
This is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Furthermore, these five dharmas take objects as their conditions;
they take the eighth consciousness as their objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
It serves as a distinct object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
Question: What is the fault?
If it takes the primary essence (*bhāva*) as its object, [what follows]?
What is meant by "differentiation of the single mode of appearance"?

If there were distinct objects of perception, then just as the five sense faculties are transformed from the six dharmas such as the fundamental consciousness into the six [objects] and the five faculties; [so too would it be here].
Furthermore, since it remains unclear upon which faculties the visual and other consciousnesses depend,
there is an obstacle in all [of these views].
According to the true meaning:
Both take the eighth consciousness as their object.
If this is so, how do you explain that they have the same object of cognition (*ālambana*) yet different modes of activity (*ākāra*)?
Although the objects are not distinct, [the modes of activity differ].
The functions of seeing and so forth are each distinct;
for instance, feeling is defined as experiencing, while perception is defined as grasping images,
and so on, because their characteristics differ.
Regarding the statement that they do not share the same characteristics,
and the mention of their being subsumed under the indeterminate (avyākṛta) nature,
the Supplement (Pū-k’uei) says:
Since it has already been clarified that this is comprised within maturation (*vipāka*) and is thus indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), why need it be further distinguished?
As for its being of an indeterminate nature,
it is because the immediately preceding explanation of the category of feeling established it as neither-painful-nor-pleasant (*aduḥkhāsukha*).
Since the sensation of neither-suffering-nor-pleasure (aduḥkhāsukhā vedanā) pertains to all three natures,
it was not yet known which nature this specific sensation subsumes; therefore,
it is now clarified once more that it is subsumed under the indeterminate nature (avyākṛta).

"One should know that the modes of activity of the remaining mental factors (*caitasika*) are likewise" means that they are categorized by analogy with the fourfold enumeration as [the case of] feeling (*vedanā*).
Third, this clarifies the mode of their functioning as mutual conditions for one another.
Within this, there is first the question, next the explanation,
and finally the restatement and conclusion.
Within the explanation, there are two parts.
First, it is explained that the ālayavijñāna and the evolving consciousnesses (pravṛttivijñānas) serve as two kinds of conditions for one another.
Second, it is explained that the evolving consciousnesses and that ālayavijñāna likewise serve as two kinds of conditions for one another.
Regarding how the ālayavijñāna serves as two kinds of conditions:
The first is the seed,
meaning that the evolving consciousnesses (pravṛttivijñāna) which can produce those [three natures] are the causal condition (hetu-pratyaya);
among the ten causes, they constitute the producing cause (janaka-hetu).
The second is that which serves as their support, namely the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
This means that the five consciousnesses arise only because the ālayavijñāna maintains the five sense faculties;
furthermore, because the ālayavijñāna gives rise to the manas, which serves as its basis, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is able to function.
This is precisely the "appropriating cause" (*parigraha-hetu*) among the ten causes,
because within the appropriating cause there are necessarily three conditions (*pratyaya*). As Ki says:
The seventh [consciousness] arises as its seeing-part (darśana-bhāga) by taking the eighth as its object;
furthermore, the seventh arises by means of the seeds within the eighth.
It possesses these two meanings.
Therefore, this statement was made.
Furthermore, regarding the passage "the various evolving consciousnesses act as two types of conditions for the ālayavijñāna," Jing says:
Because it nourishes those seeds within the present life—
meaning that based on the evolving consciousnesses, the ālayavijñāna is perfumed—
by this causal condition, the virtuous and other evolving consciousnesses further increase, become clear, and blaze forth.
These perfumations form the seeds of the designations for the three natures;
thus, these actualities serve as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*),
rather than being directed toward the substance of consciousness itself.
Those seeds have no separate substance;
they take consciousness as their nature by grasping it.
Therefore, in relation to consciousness as a whole, they are said to act as its causes and conditions.
This refers to the "generating cause" (*janaka-hetu*) among the ten causes.
Question: When active manifestations (*pravṛtti*) permeate consciousness to form seeds, do they form seeds simultaneously or at different times?
There are two explanations from the Western [tradition].
First, at the moment the perfuming occurs, it immediately becomes a seed. Second,
at the moment one understands the characteristics of the abiding and ceasing of the perfumer,
the characteristics of the arising, abiding, and production of the perfumed seed occur.
Second, it is for the sake of causing those [dharmas] to arise in a future life by gathering and planting their seeds;
that is to say, the *ālayavijñāna* perfumed by those [dharmas] is able to project the future *ālayavijñāna*.
The perfuming agent produces seeds within the fundamental consciousness that possess the potential for future existence;
these causes must wait until one has passed through a birth before they ripen.
Furthermore, the former [statement] is based on the persistence of perfuming in the present,
while the latter [statement] refers to the production of subsequent seeds through increased perfuming;
moreover, the former is based on the maturation of newly perfumed [seeds].
Later, [the argument] relies on the seeds of the foundational consciousness (ālayavijñāna) that give rise to the original existence. Jì (基) says:
"In this context, if one belongs to the school that maintains that the perfuming of seeds and their arising and ceasing are simultaneous, then this text should be taken as authoritative."
If, at another time, a certain school states regarding this passage:
"This means that the manifest perfuming consciousness, arising and ceasing simultaneously with the eighth consciousness, perfumes the eighth consciousness."
The manifest activity and the seeds do not arise and perish simultaneously;
regarding this, there are two points of contention.
One school says:
In the fifth volume of the first set,
among the seven meanings of seeds, it says:
"If a different category arises, it arises from this very thought-moment."
If the ālayavijñāna itself were not identical to this very moment,
then one would know that the active manifestation, in relation to its various [aspects] and in relation to the active manifestation itself,
arises from a different moment within its own category.
If that is so, how are the six meanings of the seeds of the Buddha-nature explained as perishing moment by moment while being co-existent?
The answer is:
this refers merely to their simultaneous arising and ceasing.
It is not that [the seed and the manifestation] arise and perish simultaneously within this very same moment.
One school (the Hōon-ji) states: "All seeds give rise to manifestations, and manifestations give rise to seeds; these must necessarily be simultaneous.
This is as explained in the *Bījārtha* (The Meaning of Seeds) and in the present text.
As in the fifth [section], the passage on the seven meanings of "seeds" and so forth,
the term "of its own kind" (svajāti) refers to the class of its own seeds.
A seed gives rise to a seed; they produce one another within their own category.
Therefore, it is not this very same moment [that arises].
If the seed is considered in relation to the manifest state, they are called "different categories."
This is precisely this very moment.
Furthermore, there is also a difference between the old seed and the new seed;
it is precisely this very moment.
Therefore, these two explanations differ in this regard.
The fourth [section] clarifies the characteristics of simultaneous operation;
first a question is posed, followed by the explanation.
The subsequent conclusion.
Within the explanation, there are two parts.
First, it clarifies their simultaneous operation.
The second part explains away doubts.
There are three aspects to simultaneous operation.
First, it clarifies how the ālayavijñāna operates simultaneously with the other consciousnesses.
The second [consciousness] operates together with two feelings,
and the third operates with consciousnesses of the three natures.
Among these, the first clarifies the fundamental treatise.
Next, the treatise on animals (tiryagyoni) is explained.

Regarding the statement that "if there is a state with mind, it should arise simultaneously with the ālayavijñāna," although the record generally mentions this for all states with mind, it applies to both states with mind and states without mind.
This is not according to reality;
it merely takes the state of being without mind as its object.
If one were to take the state of having a mind as well, [it would be incorrect].
It transforms simultaneously with two consciousnesses, or even up to [many] consciousnesses;
thus, one cannot say that it transforms only together with the single consciousness of the manas. Tai states that there are briefly two proofs for this.
It is realized that the manas-vijñāna does not exist within untainted (anāsrava) contemplation.
First, the subsequent text states:
"There are those who establish that the evolving consciousnesses (pravṛtti-vijñāna) are absent [in the state of an Arhat], but not the ālaya-vijñāna; this refers to the Arhat."
If Pratyekabuddhas, non-retrogressive Bodhisattvas, and Tathāgatas abide in the state of possessing mind,
at that time, although there is mind, it is not the ālayavijñāna.
Since this text states that the ālayavijñāna functions simultaneously with one [consciousness], namely the manas-vijñāna.
It is understood that within the uncontaminated (anāsrava) contemplation, even if there were a manas, there could be no ālayavijñāna with which it might function simultaneously.
Second, this very text states:
"For what reason? Because this manas is always associated with self-view, pride, and so forth, and functions with the aspect of cogitation (manana)."
It is clearly known that what is stated here— that manas cannot arise within the contemplation of the two emptinesses— is so;
furthermore, even if ālayavijñāna were present during a contaminated (sāsrava) contemplation,
there would be no manas that could function simultaneously with it.
By these two proofs,
it is established that the ālayavijñāna and the manas cannot function simultaneously within uncontaminated (anāsrava) contemplation;
yet it is said that they are always associated with the ālayavijñāna in both states of "with mind" and "without mind."
Regarding "arising simultaneously":
this refers to the non-conceptual absorption (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and the maturation of the non-conceptual state (*asaṃjñi-vipāka*).
Based on such textual evidence, the masters of the West [assert] that the manas consciousness exists within untainted contemplation (*anāsrava-dhyāna*).
This is not logically tenable;
for without inference (*anumāna*), the existence of the *manas* cannot be established.
There is a passage from the *Pramāṇa-samuccaya* which says:
The untainted mental consciousness has simultaneous faculties,
because it is subsumed under the sixth [consciousness],
just like the tainted mental consciousness.
The contaminated mental consciousness (sāsrava-manovijñāna) should lack a simultaneous faculty (indriya),
because it is subsumed under the sixth faculty,
just like the uncontaminated mental consciousness (anāsrava-manovijñāna).

Furthermore, the *Cheng weishi lun* (Treatise on the Establishment of Consciousness-Only) states: "For example, when the contaminated mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) of an Arhat arises, there is the manas-consciousness acting as its simultaneous basis (*sahabhū-āśraya*).
Because this is a contaminated mind, it is like the mental consciousness of an ordinary person."
That is to say, it cannot be said that this is the grasping at a person (*pudgala-grāha*) arising from an Arhat.
Jì (Guṇabhadra) says: "This contradicts the second [point] of the *Abhidharmapitaka* (*Abhidharma-kośa*).
For that [text] states: 'Furthermore, this manas is always associated with all wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral factors.'"
This excludes only the manifestation of the Noble Path;
for it is in the state of the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) and the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
Thus, this very text states that "mindless" and "possessing mind" are mutually contradictory.

Since the path of the noble ones (āryamārga) exists even in the mindless state of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), while it still functions in the state of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) who possesses a mind, there is thus a contradiction.
Based on this, there are two explanations in the West (the Indian tradition).
One interpretation states that the manas possesses only the conception of a person (pudgala-ātman) and lacks the conception of phenomena (dharma-ātman);
thus, it is correct that, according to the Abhidharma, it does not manifest during the three [meditative] states.
However, regarding the statement herein that "there is mind" or "there is no mind" in the states of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), etc.:
This refers to all other mindless states apart from the meditative attainment of cessation—
namely, the mindless states of sleep, fainting, entering the attainment of non-conception, and being born in the heaven of non-conception—
and does not refer to that which exists within the attainment of cessation itself.
Now, within the body of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) during untainted contemplation (anāsrava-dhyāna),
both vehicles enter the contemplation of the emptiness of persons (pudgala-śūnyatā),
because the seventh [consciousness] consists solely of the self of persons (pudgala-ātman).
The tainted consciousness does not function;

thus, untainted consciousness can arise. If it is argued that the seventh consciousness also functions simultaneously within the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), [it would follow that]...
Regarding the "Discourse on All Times," what is its intended meaning?
The question asks: why is it that the three times, such as the meditative attainment of cessation, do not exist?
It is said that it always functions simultaneously with the seventh consciousness.
Answer: This is based on the fact that, with the exception of three states, it functions together with it in all other states.
Even though they do not belong to the three stages [of meditative absorption],

they are also termed "concurrent. When it is subsequently stated that there are "meditative absorptions with mind" and "meditative absorptions without mind," these refer to the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), contaminated meditative absorptions (*sāsrava-samādhi*), and so forth.
It is neither the meditative absorption of cessation nor the untainted meditative absorption.
Furthermore, the second master explains that this very text is the correct one.
The manas-consciousness is always present at all times;
however, there is also a sense in which, according to the Abhidharma, it does not function during three specific periods.
This is because the seventh consciousness gives rise to both the self of persons and the self of phenomena simultaneously.
Just as when the followers of the two vehicles enter the three stages such as the untainted contemplation (*anāsrava-dhyāna*),
the manas that clings to a self does not function;
so it is when Bodhisattvas enter the three stages such as the noble path of the contemplation on the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).
Consequently, the manas that clings to phenomena (dharma-grāha-manas) does not function.
During these two periods, there is no time when the clinging to a person (pudgala-grāha) exists while the clinging to phenomena persists;
when both clingings are absent, the untainted (anāsrava) manas arises.
Now, it is said that they are "non-existent" because they exclude the two types of grasping at the outflowing (sāsrava).

This does not mean that there is no grasping at phenomena (dharma-grāha) within the contemplation of persons, nor that there is no non-outflowing (anāsrava) within the contemplation of the two emptinesses (śūnyatā).
If that is so, why does this text say that [the mental consciousness] "sometimes operates simultaneously with one [sensory consciousness]"?
The answer is: the word "sometimes" (vā) refers to the other six [sensory consciousnesses], and not to this one alone.
Not so. Because [the number] further increases by two or three and is thus indefinite, the word "or" (vā) is used.
It is not the case that the word "or" refers to the fact that the manas sometimes exists and sometimes does not exist.
For what reason is there no grasping at a person or phenomena within untainted contemplation?
The reason is as explained in the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* and the second chapter of the *Abhidharma-mahāyāna-saṃgraha*.

Regarding the statement, "Taking the ālayavijñāna as its object, it conceives of a self, gives rise to pride, and functions with the aspect of deliberation," this accords with two interpretations from the West.
The first is that of Master Rāhula.
The seventh and eighth consciousnesses take the "seeing-part" as the self and the "image-part" as the object;
this is because their seeds and so forth have already been explained as before.
Because this text takes only the *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving aspect) as its object,
there is only "I" and no "mine," and so forth. Therefore, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* and other treatises state:
Regarding "self" (*ātman*) and "what belongs to self" (*ātmīya*), there are cases where there is only the self and no "what belongs to self.
This passage from another text has been newly inserted here.
Dharmapāla’s commentary explains as follows:
By this standard, it should be known that [the view of self] takes only the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness as its object,
and does not take other portions, such as the image-portion (*nimitta-bhāga*), as its objective support. Nevertheless,
when one speaks of "self" and "what belongs to the self," etc., [it refers to this].
That is to say, one reckons the eighth [consciousness] as the self of one's own house, and that which belongs to it is "mine.
Among these, the seeds are conditioned by their own realm and not by other realms.
The unconditioned objects, the proclivities (*anuśaya*), and so forth, are as previously explained.
Furthermore, regarding the statement that "the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) takes the defiled manas as its support;
as long as the latter has not been extinguished, the former remains bound by the discernment of characteristics and cannot attain liberation," Jing says:
"The manas clings to the substantiality of persons and phenomena."
This is called the bondage of signs (*nimitta-bandhana*).
Because the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) relies upon that manas, it cannot attain purity;
this is called the great bondage of manas (*manas-mahābandhana*).

The following passage distinguishes between the two types of bondage based on the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the subjective aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
It states: "Externally, one's own body is bound by the bondage of objective aspects;
internally, one is bound by immeasurable bondages."
The "bondage of grasping at signs" (*nimitta-bandhana*) refers to the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*).
Clinging to its actual characteristics is called the bondage of signs.
The "immeasurable bondages" refer to the subjective aspect (*darśanabhāga*).
Due to the nature of being unrefined and bound by afflictions,
one is unable to abide in peace regarding any object encountered;
this is called "immeasurable bondage."
Once the manas has ceased,
the mental consciousness realizes that objects are empty and selfless;
thus, it attains liberation from the bondage of signs.
If there are further passages that contradict this, they should be interpreted in accordance with the principles set forth herein. Xuanzang (Tai) says:
"Furthermore, it is now within this context that the simultaneous arising of the ālayavijñāna and its evolving [consciousnesses] is definitively determined."
For what reason is the mental bondage (manasaḥ saṃyojanam) explained last?
There are two interpretations.
One says: because the principle [of its explanation] follows from the preceding discourse.
Furthermore, this interpretation precedes the former [explanation]:
if the ālayavijñāna is associated with the manas, it must necessarily arise together with the kliṣṭamanas,
because the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) takes the kliṣṭamanas as its support.
Therefore, it is established that there is a contaminated manas as the support for the contaminated mental consciousness;
it is not the case that in the contemplation of the emptiness of persons there is a functioning manas that is clung to,
nor does this imply the existence of an uncontaminated mental consciousness.

What is meant by this? Since this text states that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) takes the defiled *manas* as its support, it is known that the supported mental consciousness is not the untainted (*anāsrava*) mental consciousness of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*).
Furthermore, regarding the statement that "the manifestation of signs is bondage," this refers to the manifestation of signs by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

If one says that within the contemplation of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), that grasping *manas* has not yet been extinguished, then how could there be the bondage of the manifestation of signs belonging to the outflow-free consciousness (*anāsrava-vijñāna*) as its support?
Because the wisdom of selflessness takes only suchness as its object,
although this [wisdom] knows that the supported (the āśraya) is the manas of person-grasping and the supporting (the āśrita) is the contaminated mental consciousness,
when that manas ceases, all eight consciousnesses simultaneously attain liberation, not merely the mental consciousness alone.
Master Ji says: This passage arises because the preceding text states that "because the ālayavijñāna exists, the manas can exist," and thus the logical momentum (vākya-śeṣa) is established.
It is like the section on the *Maulī Bhūmi* concerning the simultaneous dependence of the mind (*manas*), where the fault of mutual dependence in their arising has not yet been resolved.
This is now clarified:
because of the existence of the manas, the sixth consciousness gives rise to the bondage of signs.
This means that because the manas conceives of the eighth consciousness as the self, [the sixth consciousness arises].
The sixth [bond] is the arising of attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) regarding objects.
Clinging to the existence of conditions such as "being" and so forth while engaging with objects is called the bond of signs (*nimittabandhana*).
The essence of the bond of signs is precisely the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*).
All objects of perception are bonds.
Furthermore, because this manas exists, all eight consciousnesses,
in perceiving their respective objects, possess the bond of perception.
As various treatises state: "The characteristic of the objective realm is that which can produce bondage.
Does this bondage arise due to the manas of dharma-grasping, or does it arise due to the manas of person-grasping?
If dharmas were grasped as real entities,
then the noble contemplation of both the followers of the Two Vehicles and those of the Mahāyāna would necessarily be with-outflows (sāsrava),
because it would invariably depend upon the grasping of dharmas as a basis.
Now, we only know that there is the grasping of the manas,
whereby the sixth consciousness and the others give rise to bondage. Why is this so?
Because this person clings to the nature of these delusions as being coarse in substance,
they give rise to the binding of the marks of other-consciousness;
