clinging to dharmas is not like this.
Therefore, they do not serve as examples.
All of these constitute bondage by way of comparing one’s own consciousness with its respective objects,
as well as through other objects acting as bonds.
Because the object of the manas conforms to the characteristics of the sixth mental consciousness (dharmavijñāna),
it gives rise to bondage; however, if it takes the untainted (anāsrava) as its object, [it does not].
The seventh is the characteristic of non-conformity.
It does not act as a binding condition for the objects of self and others.

The text explains that through mental understanding, one resolves both bondage and liberation; it is not the case that liberation occurs elsewhere than in the arising of bondage within one's own object.
Furthermore, bondage arises by taking other objects as its conditions.
Regarding the statement "either simultaneously or not simultaneously," Jing says that taking the five sense-objects collectively is called "simultaneous," and so forth.
Tài says: This explains the previous point that at one time [the mind] may be associated with three, four, or even up to seven [mental factors].
That is to say, if there are five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*), why must there necessarily be mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) as well?
To explain the intent of this question:
because the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) can also comprehend the objects of the other five consciousnesses,
there must necessarily be a mental consciousness present at the time the five consciousnesses arise.
By this principle, there are thus three,
four, or even as many as seven [consciousnesses] occurring together.
Next, it is explained that the ālayavijñāna functions simultaneously with the three feelings associated with those seven consciousnesses.
Regarding the statement that "this feeling is associated with the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) and arises depending upon them," Jing says:
"Excluding the category of feeling belonging to the *ālaya-vijñāna*,
it clarifies that the fundamental consciousness itself is associated with the three feelings which evolve together with the evolving consciousnesses."
T'ai says: "This feeling is associated with the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) and arises depending upon those evolving consciousnesses.
As for the statement regarding how it functions simultaneously with feelings that are purely painful and unmixed within the hells (*naraka*) and so forth..."
Master Ji said: "According to the *Yogācārabhūmi*, the extreme pleasure of the three dhyānas exists solely in the mental faculty (*manobhūmi*).
Likewise, the extreme suffering of the hells also exists solely in the mental faculty.
If one refers to the 'extreme' among the great hells, there is only the sensation of suffering (*duḥkhavedanā*)."
As stated in the *Purva-śāstra-saṃgraha*, it is associated with pleasure (*sukha*).
Furthermore, regarding the claim that the "Fivefold Body of Consciousness" (*pañca-vijñāna-kāya-bhūmi*) in the preceding *Maulī Bhūmi* is associated with pleasure,
such a passage does not exist.
In this passage, the word "only" (*eva*) is stated once.
This refers to the seeds; in other passages, it is also understood that [the seeds] can mature into pleasant feeling.
However, this is not the case if one refers to the manifest activities (*samudācāra*).
Therefore, it was stated previously in the fourth [section] that the four kinds of hells have no pleasant sensations (sukha-vedanā),
but rather consist for the most part of painful sensations (duḥkha-vedanā). Such are their sufferings.
This refers to the increase of suffering and does not mean that there is pleasure.
Furthermore, when it is said that death is a pleasure, this does not refer to the sensation of pleasure (*sukha-vedanā*).
Because suffering has been extinguished, it is called "pleasure," though in reality it is a painful sensation.
Furthermore, considering other minor hells, what prevents them from encountering wind as their solid food?
It must also be associated with pleasure (*sukha*).
Now, there is no contradiction in taking the resultant pleasure (*vipāka-sukha*) as the basis for this pleasure.
Furthermore, although it exists in the old *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, [it is not explicitly stated].
This is also a translation that has not yet relied upon the original [Sanskrit].
This passage does not appear in the current *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya*.
If one were to reconcile the statement regarding the hells in the *Maulī Bhūmi* as previously mentioned, it would be as follows.
Since ghosts and animals experience both suffering and pleasure,
and while the former [humans] include those who possess merit within their portion of pleasure, the latter [ghosts and animals] include those who lack merit within their portion of suffering,
they are therefore said to be "equal."
As stated in the seventeenth fascicle of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*,
although there are only three types of sensation (*vedanā*),
the term "animals and so forth" refers to a portion [of them].
Therefore, it is known that the remaining portion is purely suffering.
Third, it clarifies that the ālayavijñāna evolves simultaneously with the mind of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*). Zhongjing says:
This point is somewhat difficult.
In the Western lands (India), there are two traditional interpretations. One says:
Regarding the statement that the ālayavijñāna functions simultaneously with the mind of the three natures:
this means it can function together with the mind of the three natures from beginning to end;
it does not mean they exist at one and the same time.

This master explains that it is due to the power of the initial seeking and so forth of the first six consciousnesses that the outflows (āsrava) of the six consciousnesses are simultaneously aroused; however,
only a single momentary instance of the six consciousnesses can arise in parallel.
In succession, only the mental consciousness arises.
From the mental consciousness, the six consciousnesses arise again in succession.
Once the six consciousnesses have ceased, only the mental consciousness alone arises once more.
Furthermore, these are of a single nature without any admixture of other natures;
this interpretation contradicts the preceding one.
Previously, it was clarified that the ālayavijñāna, the seven consciousnesses, and the three types of sensation can exist simultaneously and function together at one time.

The second master says that within the state of equal defilement (*sāmkleśika*), the five consciousnesses continue in succession and can possess the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) while coexisting with the ālayavijñāna.
Master Ji further states:
Regarding the Western masters' two views on whether the five consciousnesses possess sequential conditions (*samanantara-pratyaya*) or not:
first, the position of those who maintain that there are sequential conditions holds that because the *saṃtīraṇa-citta* (investigating mind) lasts for only a single moment.
The continuity exists solely within the mind of equal outflow (*niṣyanda-citta*).
For example, when visual consciousness arises conditioned by wholesome [states] and continues until it reaches a mind of equal outflow,
a single category arises within its own continuum.
The ear-consciousness arises again and continues in a stream;
conditioned by unwholesome sounds, it proceeds in its own kind of succession,
while the preceding wholesome eye-consciousness has not yet ceased.
Because the ear does not properly discern, [the mind] subsequently arises;
thus, it arises simultaneously with the eighth [consciousness], which is neutral (*avyākṛta*), and with all three natures (*tridharmas*).
Among the five consciousnesses, it further takes up one consciousness to arise as neutral.
It should be understood that, in some cases, the seventh [consciousness] itself is [the object]. Regarding those for whom there is no immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*),
even the five sense-consciousnesses that arise as outflows (*niṣyanda*) lack continuity.
There are two explanations.
One is that the three natures arise simultaneously within a single moment of thought;
herein, the term "one kṣaṇa" is used to refer to the ultimate completion of an event.
The three natures do not arise simultaneously within a single moment of thought.
As previously stated, when a wholesome visual consciousness arises and continues until the time of the resultant flow-of-consciousness (*nisyanda-citta*),
the auditory consciousness arises as a sudden, impulsive cognition (*ābhoga-citta*).
Up until the point that an ear-consciousness arises from an unwholesome mind of similar outflow,
visual consciousness also arises;
therefore, at this single moment, both the wholesome and the unwholesome coexist.
Question: If the five consciousnesses give rise to wholesome or unwholesome states,
they must necessarily be induced by the mental consciousness (manovijñāna), just as when auditory consciousness arises.
The mental consciousness induces the arising of the unwholesome;
visual consciousness lacks such inducing power.
[If it were otherwise,] the wholesome would not arise.
The commentary states:
The initial arising of good and evil must necessarily be induced by the mind;
once they have been induced, there is no further need for induction.
Therefore, at a later time, the eye again gives rise to wholesome states.
Question: If the objects are equal, why would it take three moments for both visual and auditory consciousnesses to arise before delusion occurs?
Or, regarding attachment to an object,
what prevents it from arising immediately after an interval of one or two moments? If that were so,
the visual and auditory consciousnesses would not arise simultaneously.
The Commentary says: It is necessary to be separated by three moments (*kṣaṇa*).

This is because they belong to the same category as the five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*). Although there is craving for the object, it is because they belong to the same category as the five consciousnesses.
It cannot arise immediately after an interval of one or two moments;
however, according to another interpretation, evil may also arise after an interval of one or two *kṣaṇas*.
If that is so, there would be no simultaneous existence of the three natures.
The meaning is:
this point may indeed be true.
Therefore, when facing an object of equality, one gives rise to the three natures of mind,
as previously explained. From here on,
the second section provides an explanation of doubts and difficulties.
The textual analysis consists of four parts:
first, it clarifies that the ālayavijñāna arises simultaneously with the evolving consciousnesses (pravṛttivijñāna) yet is not associated with them;
second, it clarifies that it arises simultaneously with the evolving consciousnesses yet does not conflict with them.
Third, the various consciousnesses are distinguished according to their general and specific modes of apprehending objects;
fourth, it is established that manas arises constantly in all stages and is not contradictory to states such as the wholesome.
Regarding these four passages, each addresses potential doubts and difficulties.
The initial objection states:
"Just as a single mental factor arises,
so too do many mental concomitants arise and attain association."
Now, in the body of a single practitioner,
the eight consciousnesses and the three feelings arise simultaneously;
they ought to be associated.
Therefore, to provide a comprehensive explanation, it is said:
although it arises simultaneously with the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*),
it also arises simultaneously with mental factors (*caitta*) such as receptivity and the capacity for goodness.
This takes the preceding consciousness, together with its associated sensation, its nature, and its modes, as the subject (*dharmin*). However,
one should not state that which is associated with it as the property (*dharma*),
thereby forming the thesis (*pakṣa*) by their conjunction.
Why? Because it does not arise with the same object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
This establishes the reason, as explained below in the section on visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*).
This brings forth the commonality of the dharma and the example.
Generally, for factors to be associated (*saṃprayukta*), four criteria must be equal.
Now, although these [mental factors] arise together in this sutra, they do not share the same basis (*āśraya*)—namely, the sense organ—nor the same object (*ālambana*).
Therefore, they are not associated.
[The text] briefly omits the distinction between the different faculties (*indriya*).
The Tripiṭaka Master says:

The eye faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) and eye-consciousness (*cakṣur-vijñāna*) may be said to share the same object (*tulya-viṣaya*), but they are not called "sharing the same cognitive support" (*tulyālambana*). "Cognitive support" (*ālambana*) refers to a mental factor that possesses intentional apprehension (*sālambana*);
the eye faculty is material form (*rūpa*) and merely faces the object, so it cannot be called a "cognitive support."
As stated in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*:
"The five faculties possess only objective resistance (*viṣayapratighāta*), not cognitive resistance (*ālambanapratighāta*). Tai says:
The opponent formulates a formal argument (pramāṇa) to challenge you: "The ālayavijñāna must be associated with the three natures and the three types of feeling,
because it arises simultaneously with the evolving consciousnesses (pravṛttivijñāna), just like mental factors (caitta)."
Now, this objection is addressed by establishing two fallacies:
first, the contradiction of certainty.
The ālayavijñāna does not associate with the three natures or the three types of sensation of the evolving consciousnesses (pravṛttivijñāna),
because their objects of perception differ,
just as the visual consciousness does not associate with the eye faculty and so forth.
There are two inconclusive fallacies:
Is it because mental factors arise simultaneously that they are associated with their respective consciousnesses?
Or is it because the eye faculty and visual consciousness arise simultaneously that they cannot be associated?
An analogy cannot be entirely identical to the phenomenon it illustrates;
therefore, it is said to rely on a partial correspondence.
If it were entirely identical to the phenomenon, it would simply be that phenomenon itself.
It cannot be used as an analogy.

Question: For what reason is it that, although the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) possess both the nature of receiving (*vedanā*) and the quality of containing (*ādhāra*), they are not given the name "containing"?

Answer: Because the name "evolving consciousness" is distinct [from the storehouse consciousness], whereas the name "receiving" is common to the *ālaya-vijñāna* as well; therefore, the term "containing" is used to distinguish it.

Question: Since the term "indeterminate" (*avyākṛta*) is confused with "equanimity" (*upekṣā*), you say there is potential for confusion; however, what confusion could there be regarding the names "wholesome," "unwholesome," "suffering," and "pleasure"?
Answer: Furthermore, since these three categories are distinct, this objection does not fail to apply.
Because they are combined under the general nature of feeling (*vedanā*), the term "potential" (*yogya*) is applied as a designation.
Therefore, it is stated here that they "also accommodate and receive," rather than saying "suffering and pleasure.
Although the three natures are distinct, according to the standard principle of "receiving" (vedanā), they should correspond accordingly.
Therefore, there is no such fault. Ji further states:
"It is still expressed by means of concise terminology."
The term "evolving consciousness" (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) is self-limiting within this context;
therefore, terms such as "receptacle" (*bhājana*) and so forth are not mentioned. The second objection states:
If the body of a single practitioner were to consist of only one consciousness,
how could it not be contradictory that there are multiple consciousnesses?
This is the objection raised by the Sautrāntikas and the Sarvāstivādins.
To resolve this objection, he first cites an example as evidence.
Ji says: One should formulate the following syllogism:
"The eighth consciousness and the various [other] consciousnesses, which function simultaneously within a single body, are mutually contradictory; such is the position of this school."
The reason is stated as: "because their characteristics are each distinct.
The analogy is stated as: "just as those mental factors (caitta-dharma) arise together within a single body.
Next, two further analogies are cited.
Jingyun: The same metaphor applies to a single matter;
they arise together without contradiction.
This may also be understood in the same way. According to the ancient commentators' interpretation,
the first [section] clarifies that water and waves are not different.
Just as water, when gathered, forms waves—
this illustrates the meaning of non-separation—
it is a metaphor for how the seven evolving consciousnesses take the ālayavijñāna as their substance.
The subsequent analogy of the mirror surface illustrates the meaning of non-identity,
because the reflection is not formed by grasping the mirror surface. Tai says:
The opponent objects, saying:
"In a single body, the eight consciousnesses should be mutually contradictory and unable to function simultaneously,
because [the ālayavijñāna] is the sovereign."
Just as there cannot be multiple kings in a single country simultaneously,
the Master [Vasubandhu] points out the fallacy of mutual contradiction,
stating that within a single body and mind, consciousnesses do not contradict one another.
Because their characteristics differ,
the fact that mental factors and so forth are established within the system as being mutually non-contradictory is precisely the meaning of their simultaneous occurrence (*sahabhū*).
Master Ji said:

"This is based on the fact that the eighth consciousness is neither identical to nor different from its seeds; because these seeds exist, it is possible for the various consciousnesses to arise simultaneously.
Now, the formal inference (pramāṇa) states:"
The thesis that various consciousnesses can arise simultaneously within the eighth consciousness is established because they are neither identical nor different;
the reason is provided by the analogies of waves upon water and reflections in a mirror.
Regarding the principle of cause and effect herein:
if distinguished by their functions, they cannot be called one,
just as the nature of mental factors (*caitta*), though without differentiation, [is not a single entity].
However, because their characteristics differ,
if one were to say their substance is distinct,
[the answer is that] although the waves are many, their substance is the single water.
Therefore, the six consciousnesses and the eighth consciousness cannot be said to be different;
yet, because their causal functions are distinct, they cannot be said to be one,
just as with a single seed.
Cause and effect are not established in themselves,
for they are ultimately established only in relation to their counterparts, such as dust; thus,
their essence is of a single nature.
If they were different, the relationship of cause and effect could not be established;
therefore, one cannot say they are different.
This is because, for example, water does not produce fire due to their difference in nature.
The principle here is likewise.
As stated by Asaṅga and others in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*,
the six consciousnesses and so forth are taken as having distinct, independent entities.
Furthermore, there is a dharma that is itself a single entity;
these two meanings are distinct.
Herein, the explanation is based upon the Middle Way.
Second, both individually and collectively are non-apprehending. Regarding both locations, taking them together is likewise correct.
Third, there is a doubt as follows:
How is it that the various consciousnesses apprehend their respective objects without contradiction?
To resolve this doubt,
the text first clarifies how the visual consciousness apprehends its objects both collectively and individually.
Second, the three types of consciousness;
third, the body-consciousness apprehending its object;
fourth, by analogy, the mental consciousness.
The five fetters (saṃyojana) manifest as non-contradictory. Tái says:
"In the Mahāyāna, it is like the visual consciousness (cakṣurvijñāna), which at a single moment (ekakṣaṇa) apprehends multiple colors such as blue, yellow, and so forth."
There are various modes of engagement, such as blue, yellow, and so forth;
their apprehension of characteristics differs, yet they do not contradict one another.
This is explained at length, and it is the same even for the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
One should know that it is not contradictory for the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) to coexist with the various [evolving] consciousnesses. Bei states:
"The doctrine of the third master in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* corresponds to this treatise."
That is to say, as that treatise states regarding the visual consciousness apprehending form, there are four masters' interpretations:
first, the interpretation of distinct objects;
second, the interpretation of indistinct collective apprehension.
Regarding the discernment of conditions:
the three types of understanding [of the three realms] take color-form collectively as their object; the discernment of individual color-form takes it individually as its object.
This should be understood according to its true meaning:
when a collection of many forms is present, many consciousnesses arise with respect to a single form;
if they are not collected, then a single consciousness arises conditioned by a single form.
The fourth doubt asks:

How can the nature of the ālayavijñāna be indeterminate (avyākṛta), while simultaneously functioning in conjunction with the three natures (kuśala, akuśala, and avyākṛta) of both concentrated and distracted consciousnesses?
It is not at all contradictory.
To resolve this doubt,
the preceding explanation is cited as evidence.
The nature of manas is a concealed and distracted mind;
it is compatible with states of meditative concentration and wholesome states alike,
without any contradiction.
The ālayavijñāna and the evolving consciousnesses arise simultaneously without mutual contradiction;
what is there to wonder at? Ji says:
The analysis of the manas through its various aspects can be understood from the section on the "virtues" (guṇa).
Regarding its taking the eight [consciousnesses] as the self and what belongs to the self,
there are two explanations.
First, to take the five aggregates as the self,
and to take what is conditioned by them as "mine"—
this is not the correct principle.
Because they take distinct objects,
two [types of] views are taught:
namely, directly taking "I" as its object is the view of self (ātmadṛṣṭi).
Regarding the notions of "I" and "mine" within my own house, one asks:
how can two mental states arise within a single moment of thought?
The explanation says:
If the sixth consciousness still gives rise to cognitions of all objects,
what prevents the manas from doing so?
This interpretation is correct.
Furthermore, the aspect of seeing (*darśana-bhāga*) is taken as the self,
and the aspect of the object (*nimitta-bhāga*) is taken as the objective realm;
the remaining two [aspects] correspond to the treatises on the two categories of existence.
Or, according to the correspondence with the number nineteen and so forth:
at what time is the third fruit abandoned?
Is it suppressed by the mundane path or not?
As explained in Master Jùn’s *Chapter on Manas*,
this manas is also superior to the preceding discussion on the simultaneous functioning of the various consciousnesses;
for those who have not yet understood that, this is provided as a further clarification.
The aforementioned source states:
"If one does not understand whether [the mind] is with thought or without thought,
nor whether it pertains to the meditative or non-meditative stages."
Because it does not contradict [the categories of] wholesome and unwholesome,
the present passage is called "repeated determination.
This is because it explains that the six consciousnesses take both self and other as their objects, as stated in the preceding text.
Therefore, the treatise says: "Furthermore, this was stated previously.
The fifth section clarifies the characteristics of transcending the flow and returning to cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Within it, there is first the question, then the explanation, and finally the conclusion.
Within this, there are three parts:
first, clarifying the establishment of the transcendence of the stream;
second, clarifying the mental orientations (*manasikāra*) of entering, penetrating, and practicing cultivation.
The establishment of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) through the three knowledges (*vidyā*) occurs within the section on "Transcending the Currents.
First, the thesis is briefly established.
This refers to all that transcends the stream.
Why is this so? The following questions and answers provide a detailed analysis in seven points.
When reaching the conclusion at the end, only five phrases are cited;
the third and fourth are not cited.
As for what is called "seven phrases":
First, the fundamental basis of sentient beings;
second, the fundamental basis of the receptacle world;
third, the fundamental basis for the mutual arising of sentient beings.
Because all sentient beings are mutually related as *adhipati-pratyaya* (dominant conditions) and so forth. Jing says:
"This passage accords with [the view of] Dharmapāla, that one's own *ālayavijñāna* transforms into and conditions the sense organs and objects of others, yet does not grasp or maintain them."
If it does not transform and give rise to the sense faculties,
objects, and so forth of another, how can it be said that one perceives suffering, pleasure, and the like arising in the body of another?

This occurs because the seeds of the common characteristics (sāmānya-lakṣaṇa) of one's own body transform, within the locus of another's body, into the sense faculties and objects of that other's body, whereby the mind arises and apprehends them for itself.
In fact, it is subsumed under the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*),
yet its characteristics are subsumed under sentient beings (*sattva*).
Ji states that there are two explanations regarding this in the West.
One school, [the Sākāravāda], maintains that the eighth [consciousness] transforms upward into another body;
the second school, Dharmapāla, holds otherwise.

That is to say, the eighth [consciousness] undergoes two types of transformation: it transforms into the sense organs and so forth, and it causes the view of self and other afflictions to arise within the body.
This is the maturation of uncommon collective karma;
the second is also the maturation of common collective karma,
such as causing others to see [the Buddha] and so forth.
Therefore, it is called the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*).
If, as Ratnacandra claims, [the seeds] also transform into another's body,
then the five sense organs and consciousnesses that serve as the supports for that other's body must likewise arise from the seeds of one's own body.
If that is so, why would consciousness not arise from its own seeds?
It should be the same as [the case of] the sense faculties.
To formulate this in a formal syllogism (*pramāṇa*):
The eye-consciousness of another's body should arise from one's own seeds,
because it is either the eye-faculty or the eye-consciousness of that other's body,
just like the eye-faculty of that other's body.
If the sense-faculty that serves as the basis for another’s body-consciousness were not directly produced by oneself, how would it differ from my own?
It is because the eighth consciousness transforms [the faculties] with the other person acting as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).

However, transforming them into another's body merely means they are subsumed within the external vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*); it does not mean that the actual sense-faculties and consciousnesses of another are transformed.
Relying on transformations, they support the sense organs and their objects;
thus, the sixth consciousness may be reckoned as a sentient being and so forth.
Within this, there are two types of karma.
That is to say, there are the common and the uncommon.
Within the common, however, there are two types:
namely, the common-within-the-common.
Common and uncommon: for example,
the external container-world is common because it is experienced through the collective conditions of others.
This is called "common among the common," such as clothing, vessels, and so forth,
which are used exclusively for one's own purposes.
Although its function and meaning are shared [with others],
its own enjoyment of karmic fruition is superior and is thus called "unshared" within the shared.
Within this unshared category, there are also two types.
This refers to that which is uncommon among the uncommon,
and that which is common among the uncommon;
for example, one's own visual faculty.
The consciousnesses of others do not rely upon them; they rely solely upon their own respective consciousnesses.
This is called "unshared among the unshared.
Furthermore, the sensory bases (*āśraya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) that support these faculties are produced by the unique karma of each individual.
However, this is also the eighth transformation of another;
that is, it is common among those who do not share [the same mental continuum].
Question: Just as what is transformed by the visual consciousness within one's own body is not seen by the mental consciousness and so forth, [is this case the same?]
How much more so for others?
How is it called "common within the common" and "uncommon within the common"?
The commentary states:
However, as for those that are exclusively non-common according to principle,
they are all transformations produced by the eighth consciousness itself; others do not experience them.
Now, based on their similarity:
just as in that case, it is for one's own enjoyment alone and serves no purpose for others.
It is called "unshared among the unshared.
Although the external container world, though transformed by oneself, is not for the use of others,
there is nevertheless a sense of similarity within its enjoyment.
It is said that because it is shared by all, it is called "common karma.
The remaining two phrases should be explained accordingly.
This refers to the fact that even in the present, one transforms the actual sense faculties and so forth of other bodies.
Furthermore, it is said:
regarding the interpretations of the two masters,
one says "transformation."
The eighth [consciousness] transforms by relying on the bodies of others.
The second [treatise] states:
"The visual consciousness relies upon that which is transformed by the eighth [consciousness] and further transforms it."
If that is so, what is incorrect?
Could it be that because the eye is the supporting basis (āśraya), one therefore speaks of them as distinct?
These principles should be examined in detail by those with discernment.
Fourth, it is capable of maintaining all seeds.
Fifth, in the present life, it is the essence of the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*).
Because they repay prior causes.
Furthermore, why are these six also the productive causes for future suffering?
Because they maintain the seeds and draw forth what is to come.
Seventh, regarding the present origin of suffering (*samudaya-satya*) as the cause of arising:
because afflictions and karma arise from delusion regarding the manifest consciousness, it is called the "present cause of origin.
Second, the explanation of the mental engagements (*manasikāra*) of entering, penetrating, and cultivating.
In the first part, the entry into and realization [of the path] is clarified;
in the latter part, the cultivation of mental attention (*manasikāra*) is clarified.
Within the former, there are again two sections.
The first section concerns initial entry and thorough penetration;
the latter explains and resolves doubts and difficulties.
Within the former, there are five phrases.

Regarding the initial statement that the *ālayavijñāna* encompasses the seeds of wholesome dharmas such as the "section on the determination of liberation" (*vimuktipariccheda*) and so forth, which are not causes of the truth of origination (*samudayasatya*) because they are contrary to the process of transmigration (*pravṛtti*):
Jing says, "Before the seven stages of expedient means (*saptaprayoga*), one resolves to seek liberation."
This is the stage conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*).
The first three preparatory stages (*pūrvaprayoga*) are called the stages conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).
The four [stages] beginning with "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) are precisely the stages of penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).
These two roots of goodness involve a distaste for the realms of birth and death and a pursuit of the Noble Path;
therefore, they are not the Truth of Origination (samudaya-satya). Thus, the *Maulī Bhūmi* clearly distinguishes the twelve links [of dependent origination].
It is exclusively neither-learner-nor-non-learner because it follows the cycle of saṃsāra; however,
the *Mokṣabhāgīya* and other such treatises designate it as "learner" (śaikṣa).
Because it is contrary to the process of saṃsāra and does not consist of the factors of existence (bhavāṅga),
it is not the truth of origination (samudayasatya).
However, in other places it is said that the three faculties— such as "the faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown'" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*)—
are exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*) and constitute the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*).

For instance, the seven types of preparatory practices prior to the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), as well as the Path of Seeing itself, constitute the essence of the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown."
Furthermore, texts in other locations state that the wholesome factors conducive to liberation (mokṣabhāgīya) pertain to all three realms, as well as to those that are unconditioned by any realm;
whereas the wholesome factors conducive to penetration (nirvedhabhāgīya) pertain to the realms of form and formlessness, as well as to those that are unconditioned.
Is this not contradictory? There is such an objection.

According to the interpretation in the Western [Indic] lands, the uncontaminated seeds of the three vehicles are established by their very nature (*dharmatā-prakṛti-siddha*); following the arousal of the thought of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*), they exist throughout the stages of the eight aids to liberation (*aṣṭau vimokṣabhāgīyāni*) and the stage conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).
It is precisely at this stage that these seeds are also called the "factors conducive to liberation" (*mokṣa-bhāgīya*) and so forth.
These two roots of goodness are the very substance of the faculty of "knowing what is not yet known" (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*).
Therefore, it is said that the three untainted faculties (*anāsravendriya*) are exclusively comprised within the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*), being entirely untainted.
Furthermore, regarding the statement that the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) pertain to both those bound to the three realms and those not so bound:
their essence is contaminated (*sāsrava*) and thus bound to the three realms;
however, because they involve a distaste for birth and death (*saṃsāra*), they do not invariably bring about rebirth.
They are called "unbound" (*apratisaṃyukta*).
The factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) pertain to both the realms of form and formlessness as well as being unbound;
the meaning is also as explained previously.

Question: If the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) were contaminated (*sāsrava*), being bound to the realm of pleasure (*sukhāvacara*), they would necessarily induce the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga*). If they were such links, [how could they lead to liberation?]
If the twelve links [of dependent origination] also possess this quality of being "in training" (*śaikṣa*),
why is it definitively stated that they are neither "in training" nor "beyond training" (*aśaikṣa*)?
The explanation says:
If these are with outflows (sāsrava), they generally induce both collective and individual retributions and enter into the twelve links [of dependent origination];
however, the factors conducive to liberation (mokṣabhāgīya) and so forth do not.
Because of weariness with birth and death, [ignorance] cannot pull [the other factors] together as a whole;
yet its essence is still tainted (*sāsrava*), and thus it still brings about individual roots.
Since it possesses such advancement and retreat, it is not one of the twelve links.
Therefore, the twelve links [of dependent origination] cannot be called "training. Ji says:

"The current interpretation holds that the three preparatory practices, such as the five stages of mental abiding (*pañca-viṣaya-sthiti-citta*), are precisely the essence of the stage conducive to liberation (*mokṣa-bhāgīya*)."
Since these are all prior to the stages of penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*),
they are called "conducive to the stages conducive to penetration" (*ānulomika-nirvedhabhāgīya*).
The same applies to the stage of liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*).
From the stage of wisdom derived from hearing onwards, it is called the "factor conducive to liberation" (*mokṣabhāgīya*).
Prior to this, [the practices] such as upholding the twelve divisions of the scriptures are categorized as innate virtue (*upapattilābhika-kuśala*);
therefore, they constitute the preparatory application (*prayoga*) for that factor conducive to liberation.
It is not part of the stage conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*). The realm of liberation (*vimuktidhātu*) pertains to all nine stages;
there is an explicit textual authority for this.
The *Nirvedhabhāgīya* (stages conducive to penetration) are said by the Tripiṭaka Master to extend through the seven stages:
the four form realms and the three formless realms.
If that is so, how is it that the subsequent explanation regarding the six types of clear realization (*abhisamaya*) states that three arise based on five stages?
Therefore, we know that the levels of penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) are bound to the five stages of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
This is because the first three preparatory practices (*prayoga*) constitute the levels of penetration.
The five contemplations for settling the mind (*pañca-viṣkambhana-bhāvanā*) and so forth belong to the distracted mind and are thus associated with the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); therefore,
they pertain to all seven stages.
Since the four roots of goodness, such as "heat" (uṣmagata) and so forth,
exist only in the form realm (rūpadhātu),
there is no contradiction in their being based on either three or five [foundations].
Regarding the statement here that [these roots] are not causes for the Truth of Origination and so forth:
if Vijayasena says, "These factors conducive to liberation (mokṣabhāgīya) are also roots of goodness (kuśalamūla)."
Although its nature is contaminated, it is skillfully embraced by expedient means such that the seeds of merit-related virtue and so forth increase, bringing about the ripening fruit;
yet, it remains conducive to the uncontaminated.
It cannot truly induce the fruit of suffering, which is the universal root of birth and death; therefore,
it is said not to be the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*), as [held by] Ratnacandra and others.
That is to say, by the power of the untainted seeds,
they cause the manifest skillful dharmas of the outflowing realm, such as the roots of goodness pertaining to merit and so forth, to function as expedient means.
Two dharmas increase.
The second line states: "Because all other worldly roots of goodness arise from this."
Regarding "becoming even more brilliant and flourishing," Jingyun says:
this refers to the worldly portion of merit and roots of goodness.
Because it is assisted and guided by the superior portion of understanding and so forth,
it becomes increasingly bright and flourishing. Jì (基) says:
Because they have repeatedly practiced preparatory wholesome states (*prayoga-kuśala*), they thoroughly comprehend cause and effect; therefore, they are "clear-sighted" (*vidarśana*).

If so, those such as Rāhula also possess clear comprehension regarding present preparatory wholesome states, tainted wholesome states (*sāsrava-kuśala*), and merit-related states (*puṇyabhāgīya*) and so forth.
Regarding the third point,
"by these causes and conditions, up to the point of swiftly attaining establishment," Jing says:
This clarifies the seeds of merit.
Through the guidance and support of the factors conducive to liberation and so forth,
they further become intense and flourishing conditions.
One is then able to gather and nurture the seeds of one's own portion of merit, causing them to increase and reach fulfillment.
Ji (基) says:
"In this context, it is by virtue of liberation and so forth acting as causes and conditions."

Now, the seeds of worldly merit, such as wholesome [karma] and so forth, which consist of nominal expressions (*nāma-vyavahāra*) and indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) seeds, possess the capacity for transformation;
the seeds of wholesome karma and so forth possess the power for transformation;
and the seeds of the roots of goodness conducive to liberation (*mokṣa-bhāgīya-kuśala-mūla*) are swiftly brought to fulfillment.
That which establishes [the result] is capable of increasing and bringing about the superior production of the fruit.
Furthermore, it causes the seeds of the wholesome factors conducive to merit (*puṇyabhāgīya*) and so forth to be swiftly established.
Within this context, "newly perfumed" and "original" have two meanings.
Regarding the fourth point, which states: "Furthermore, by virtue of these seeds, those various wholesome dharmas arise with increased clarity and vigor," Jing explains:
"This clarifies that the seeds of the merit-portion (*puṇyabhāga*) are capable of producing manifest activity (*samudācāra*) as their outflowing fruit (*niṣyandaphala*)."
This means that because the seeds of its own kind within the category of merit increase,
it causes the manifestation of merit to arise with greater clarity and intensity. Jī says:
Because of the seeds of the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) and so forth,
wholesome phenomena subsequently arise with increasing clarity through one's own actual practice.
Furthermore, it is said that this refers to the actual practice of the factors conducive to merit (*puṇyabhāgīya*).
If that is so, how does this differ from the previous [explanation] regarding the increasing intensity of the transformation?
It is said: because it is superior to the former, it increases moment by moment.
Regarding the fifth [point], it says: "Furthermore, next, it is able to induce even the various ripening fruits (*vipāka-phala*)."
Jingyun explains that this clarifies the superiority of the ripening fruit (*vipāka-phala*).
That is to say, the aforementioned seeds of the meritorious portion do not merely produce the present concordant fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*);
they also bring about the ripening fruit to be experienced in the future.

Jizang says: "This precisely clarifies the meaning of wholesome karma pertaining to the category of merit (*puṇyabhāgīya*); it does not refer to wholesome karma pertaining to the category of liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) and so forth.
Nevertheless, it is not that these do not produce distinct retributions."
The following section addresses and subdues potential objections. The intent of the objection is as follows:
the Master previously stated that the ālayavijñāna is the cause of defilement.
Why, then, is it further described as the cause of cessation?
If both the obstacle and its remedy exist within a single consciousness,
would this not be contradictory?
The Master of the Treatise cites two sūtras below to provide the answer.
First, he cites the *Bīja-sūtra*:
"If within a single consciousness both affliction and liberation manifest..."
These two dharmas are mutually contradictory;
however, the principle that the seeds of purity reside within a single consciousness remains unimpaired.
Therefore, it is said that the Bhagavat taught there are eighteen *dhātus*.
This is because within the *ālayavijñāna* there are various *dhātus*.
A *dhātu* has the meaning of both "seed" and "cause."
Furthermore, as it is said in the sūtra regarding the akṣa fruit,
because they are separated,
a second sūtra is cited.
The Tripitaka Master said:
"In the Western Regions, I have seen akṣa fruits;
they resemble the *wúshízi* (jujube) used here for dyeing boots."
In the Western Regions, these are taken to be dyed or pressed to extract oil;
as there is no corresponding name here [in China] to translate it,
the term "akṣa" is retained.
Second, the cultivation of mental attention (*manasikāra*) is explained.
This section first presents the heading and subsequently provides the explanation.

Within the explanation, it is first clarified that those of the three vehicles who have not yet seen the truths, prior to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), take only the evolving consciousnesses as their object and practice the contemplation of the four truths.
When practicing mental attention (*manasikāra*),
one has not yet attained penetration into the principle of the *ālayavijñāna*; thus,
when contemplating the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*), one contemplates it only in a general manner.
Because the ālayavijñāna is not yet known,
it is said that [the practitioner] takes the evolving consciousnesses as their object.
Next, it is explained that once one has entered the Path, one is able to penetrate the ālayavijñāna.
Regarding the statement "or entering the śrāvaka’s right state of departure from birth" (*samyaktva-niyāma*),
Jing says: "The old [translation] refers to the 'noble nature' (*ārya-dhātu*) as the 'right state' (*samyaktva*)."
The nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) is called "wrong nature.
Now, upon entering the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), one abandons the wrong and attains the right;
yet, one shall still undergo boundless birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
Now, upon entering the Path of Seeing, with the exception of seven more births,
one attains the cessation of remaining births, transcends and departs from the state of ordinary birth.
Now, in the Western lands, it is explained that one contemplates the principle of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
This is called the "right nature" (*samyaktva*).
Because it is said to be "departing from birth," it refers to the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Afflictions (*kleśa*) are the root of birth and death.
It is like raw food remaining undigested in the stomach, which serves as the root of all diseases;
using this as a metaphor, the term "birth" (jāti) refers to the delusions of view (dṛṣṭi-kleśa).
Since one now severs these delusions of view, it is called "separation from birth" (vairāgya).

distraction and non-distraction; that which should be cultivated and that which should not be cultivated.
Regarding liberation and non-liberation,
and heedfulness and heedlessness:
in this second characteristic, the preceding is first restated to introduce the subsequent.
The second section provides the formal analysis.
Within this, first the defects are analyzed,
followed by an explanation of how, due to the existence of these defects, epidemics and other calamities arise.
When one is killed or bound due to the manifestation of greed, it is called an offense in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavipāka*).
When one falls into the evil realms due to greed, it is called an offense in future lives (*sāmparāyikavipāka*).
Those who suffer from epidemics [experience] offenses in the present life.
That which is "accidental" refers to offenses in future lives;
that which is "calamitous" refers to offenses in both the present and future lives;
and that which is "afflictive" refers to the mental and physical suffering of grief.
Regarding Master Ji’s statement that there are four [calamities], such as pestilence and so forth:
this is as the Tripiṭaka Master says—
that the first three constitute the "three harms."
The latter one is mental distress and suffering.

Within it, Jing says: "By means of the mind that accords with reality (*yathābhūta-citta*), one understands that the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is originally without characteristics, thereby realizing that suchness (*tathatā*)."
This is called skill in the mind.

To understand, through knowledge of things as they are (yathābhūtajñāna), that phenomena such as the defiled and purified states of the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) evolve from causes and conditions,
is called the distinction of skill in knowing the evolution of the mind.
Jizang said:
"Based on the fact that what is conceptually constructed has no coming and no going and is by nature in nirvāṇa,
one who is able to know, in accordance with reality, the mind that realizes the suchness of the dharmatā at the moment of realization is called 'skillful.'"
It is called "differentiation" because it is not [identical to] the dependent nature and so forth.
The mind that takes the three natures as its object—
this dependent phenomenon— is not a non-existent thing.
To observe and know that this mind arises in dependence upon others is called the transformation of the mind.
To be able to know this truly and not give rise to the grasping of pervasive conceptualization is called skillfulness.
The observation that differs from the preceding one is called "differentiation.
Furthermore, it is explained that dependently originated phenomena do not exist, yet they appear to exist; they are provisionally designated as existing.
When these phenomena are severed, one realizes suchness;
this is called skillfulness in the transformation of the mind.
"Transformation" (parāvṛtti) means cessation.
Realizing the mind of suchness,
one extinguishes the dependent nature and the thoroughly imagined nature.
The essence of nature is non-existent;
in the contemplation of phenomena, there is only existence.
That which the mind clings to cannot be severed.
One who does not realize suchness is merely called "skillful in mind.
Next, the gains and losses regarding purity are explained.
First, regarding those who find peace and happiness in the fruit:
One attains bodhi and nirvāṇa.
Regarding mastery over causes:
having caused the mind to find joy, one does not crave or indulge in negligence.
Furthermore, precisely because of the prior cultivation of the mind,
one attains ultimateity at the time of the fruit, whereby there is peace and happiness;
during the causal stage, one exercises mastery over the control of the three natures.
The third response to the objection.
Zhongjing says: "The intent of this objection is as follows."
The Master of the Treatise proceeds to distinguish the skillful differentiation of well-cultivating the mind.
This accords with the words of the Blessed One: "One should, with profound diligence and vigor, examine the mind in accordance with reality. This statement is consistent with the present context.
Furthermore, according to another sutra regarding the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna),
it is said that one must dwell upon the body and cultivate contemplation of the body, and so on, up to dwelling upon phenomena and cultivating contemplation of phenomena;
this constitutes the universal contemplation of body, sensation, mind, and phenomena.
Does this not contradict what was stated previously?
Therefore, what is the underlying intention (*abhiprāya*) in saying this?
The answer is: it is to demonstrate that the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) consist solely in the contemplation of the mind.
This provides a general response to the preceding sutra;
although it mentions the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena collectively,
its intent is solely to observe the mind.
The following is a detailed analysis.
Regarding "observing the mind as that which appropriates":
it means observing that physical body as that which is capable of appropriating the mind.
Therefore, it is called "contemplating the body.
Regarding "contemplating the mind as that which experiences":
this refers to contemplating the sense in which that mind-king is capable of experiencing.
This is precisely what is called "contemplating the mind-king" (*cittarāja*) as discernment;
it is termed "contemplating the mind.
Regarding the contemplation of the defilement and purity of the mind, one contemplates the meaning of the defilement and purity of that mind-king.
This is precisely what is called "contemplating phenomena" (*dharmānupaśyanā*). The phrase "only for the purpose of observation" concludes and clarifies the intent of the sutra.
Master Ji states: "This serves solely to sever the mind that clings to pleasure, purity, permanence, and self."
Because one gives rise to the perception of actual impurity and so forth regarding objective phenomena (*dharma*).
Some say that through the application of mindfulness to the mind (*cittasmṛtyupasthāna*), one attains the object.
In this context, the preceding statement refers to the universal presence of the groups of consciousness (*vijñānakāya*) within the mind.
Now it is said that one should simply cultivate profound and courageous diligence within the mind;
hence this objection arises. Furthermore, the four inversions are as previously stated.
The eighth [inversion] states that attachment to precepts and rituals is the inversion of regarding suffering as pleasure.
The view of grasping at views is the inversion of purity;
the extreme view is partially the inversion of permanence,
and the view of self is the inversion of selfhood.
The *Xiányán* (Exposition of the Manifest) states: "Since all four inversions are collectively inversions of view, they are all [inversions] of the mind;
for the sake of eliminating these, the fourth [section] cites a sūtra as an explanation."
He then cites two sūtras. Regarding the passage,
"Abiding in the three modes of practice and performing the six correct practices, one accomplishes much within the Teacher’s instruction," this cites the first sūtra.
This refers to the explanation following the term "abiding. Jing says:
"Abiding in liberation" means abiding [in it].
The liberation consisting of the awakening and nirvāṇa of the three vehicles, which is freedom from bondage, is called "liberation.
When it is realized through wisdom, it is called "abiding in the abode of liberation.
As for "abiding in the gates of liberation":
These are the gates of liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
If one distinguishes the three liberations according to the perspective of the established truths (*vyavasthāna-satya*),
then that which is characterized by emptiness and selflessness is called the liberation of emptiness.
The two aspects of suffering and impermanence, along with four aspects each for origin and the path, are termed "wishlessness" (apraṇihita).
The four lower aspects of cessation are termed "signlessness" (animitta).
If established according to the non-conceptual truth (avyavasthāpana-satya), a single true suchness (tathatā) possesses these three meanings.
Just as being free from persons and phenomena is the gate of emptiness (*śūnyatā*),
being free from the ten signs is called signlessness (*animitta*),
and being free from the conceptual seeking of objective spheres is called wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).
When the wisdom of realization in a single thought-moment realizes suchness,
according to its distinct meanings, it is said to possess the three liberations.
Master Ji states that this is as explained in the second chapter of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*.
If one says that emptiness and so forth are not empty, and cultivation and so forth are not non-cultivation,
this then encompasses the three wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation, as well as both the outflowing (sāsrava) and the outflow-free (anāsrava).
If one speaks only of the samādhis such as emptiness,
these refer exclusively to the wisdom born of cultivation,
which encompasses both the tainted and the untainted.
If it is said that the gates of liberation, such as emptiness and so forth,
consist solely of untainted cultivated wisdom (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*),
then these three gates of liberation would now enter only the untainted state upon seeing the truths (*darśanamārga*).
Within the inclusion of the six lower correct practices, these are subsumed under the two paths of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).
Furthermore, those who abide in the dharmas that lead to the gates of liberation are those who abide in the ten skillful means prior to the path of seeing.
Furthermore, there is dwelling in liberation;
dwelling in the truth of cessation, which is nirvāṇa;
and dwelling in the gates of liberation.
This refers to the Truth of the Path.
Since Nirvana is manifested by depending upon it,
it is called a "gate."
Regarding "abiding in the dharmas that lead to the gates of liberation":

this refers to the middle path of the truth of cessation, such as the vision of the truths, which is induced by the three types of mundane wisdom (*trividhā prajñā*) belonging to the stage prior to the [first] ground (*bhūmi*).
Next, the practice of the six right practices (*ṣaḍ-samyak-pratipatti*) is explained.
That "the auspicious clouds move without interval" refers to the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*).
This wisdom of hearing arises directly from the teachings.
This is called "uninterrupted practice.
For one who practices the contemplation of wholesome sensations,
this is the practice of wisdom derived from reflection.
The arising of roots of goodness induced by the practice of cultivation refers to the practice of contaminated wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).
These are the practices of the three types of wisdom.
That is to say, one abides in the dharma-abiding that leads to the gates of liberation by subsuming what preceded;
for this is likewise a preparatory practice prior to the path of vision (darśanamārga) of the three vehicles.
It is the practice of discerning the truths while remaining free from all attachment to flavors.
This refers to those who, within the two kinds of paths of vision— those with signs and those without signs—
of the three vehicles, are free from all attachment to flavors and practice without overweening pride regarding the analytical establishment and non-establishment of the truths.
"Penetration" refers to the practice and study of the path of cultivation of the three vehicles;
previously one attained the path of seeing,
and now one attains the path of cultivation.
This immediately eliminates the overweening pride (*adhimāna*) of claiming to have attained what has not yet been attained.
These two lines subsume the preceding dwellings in the gates of liberation,
because they both pertain to the paths of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).
The practice of correct and pure enjoyment refers to the practice of those beyond training (aśaikṣa) in the three vehicles;
it is called "pure" because it is free from defilement and has reached its cessation.
Realizing the bliss of nirvāṇa is termed "enjoyment" (*paribhoga*);
this subsumes the previously mentioned abiding in liberation,
because they share the same essence.
Master Ji says that the initial interpretation is largely the same.
Furthermore, he interprets "uninterrupted practice" as the uninterrupted cultivation within the seven stages of expedient means.
Having properly received and reflected upon [the teachings],
and having immediately practiced the path of seeing (darśanamārga),
one now attains the untainted (anāsrava).
Therefore, it is said that they are "well-received.
What is produced by cultivation refers to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*),
because it arises based on the roots of goodness produced through cultivation.
Within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), one becomes free from the desires of the three realms.
This is precisely the time of becoming free from the desires of the lower realm;
being freed from the desire for the form realm is called the practice of discerning the truths (*satyavipaśyanā*).

To discern by means of the principles of the Truths while free from desire for the formless realm is called being without overweening pride; it is like a monk with overweening pride who, having attained the fourth dhyāna, claims it to be the fruit of arhatship.
This refers to one who, having become free from desire for the formless realm, attains the untainted state without giving rise to overweening pride;
likewise, it refers to one who, having already attained freedom from desire for the form realm, does not give rise to overweening pride.
These all pertain to the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga).
However, it receives its name based on its preeminence within a single realm;
this is not as previously explained.
When one subsequently attains the fruit of arhatship (aśaikṣa-phala), it is termed "rightly pure conduct" (samyak-śuddha-caryā).
Because one attains the six modes of constant abiding (*ṣaḍ-āveṇika-vihāra*),
the preceding liberations may also be sequentially assigned accordingly:
the first [liberation] above corresponds to the third [liberation] mentioned previously.
The four in the middle are the second of the preceding [set],
spoken in terms of the period of increase;
the sixth is the first of the preceding [set].
Alternatively, these latter five may collectively apply to both of the preceding two.
Next, he cites the second sutra for explanation.
Jing says: "The one who receives is the one who relinquishes and gives."
Just as Mahākāśyapa went on his almsround in successive order to benefit the poor,
he thus sacrificed his own body as a field for merit.
Receiving food and drink from another is called "giving to a recipient";
it may also be observed that one gives immediately upon seeing a recipient.
This is called giving to a recipient.
Second is giving through renunciation;
thus, one can understand the donor's practice of giving.
The fruits of giving are also twofold.
First, one attains great wealth;
this is the first fruit of giving.
Sacrificing one's own body is the field;
giving wealth to the recipient is the gift.
Thus, one obtains great wealth in the present life.
Because one obtains the object of the gift.
If it is said that one gives immediately upon seeing a recipient,
this will result in great wealth in the future.
Second, those who attain the resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) in the enjoyment that is the outflow (*niṣyanda*) of these [results] experience the fruit of the donor’s giving:
by relinquishing wealth, they will in the future obtain abundant wealth once again.
This is called "attaining the outflow" (*niṣyanda*).
Because of this, one is subsequently able to use it oneself or give it to others;
this is called "superior resolve regarding enjoyment" (*paribhoga-adhimukti*).
Ji says that he recounts two interpretations from the Tripiṭaka Master.
One states: "It is like one who begs for food.
This is identical to Master Jing’s initial interpretation.
Second, it is said that having received the wealth of others, one practices giving;
this refers to giving by means of transformation.
As for the gift of Dharma, its nature as a gift is self-evident.
Furthermore, it destroys one's own stinginess;
therefore, when one enjoys wealth oneself,
the recipient effectively gives it to one's own person by relinquishing it.
This is called giving to a recipient;
it is given even to one's own servants,
as all such acts are performed with a mind of generosity.
This refers to obtaining wealth in the future and using it for oneself as the result of a dominant resolve (*niṣyanda-adhimukti-phala*).
Second, giving to others.
One attains great wealth. Furthermore,
as explained previously regarding the first two types of giving,
both result in the attainment of great wealth as their ripened fruit (*vipāka-phala*).
Among these, the fact that stinginess can still lead to the enjoyment of reputation and so forth is called the concordant fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*).
This is the fourth principle of proof (*upapatti-sādhana-yukti*),
which definitively discerns causes and conditions.
First, the general exposition is presented, followed by the formal analysis.
Within the formal analysis, the first part clarifies the reasoning that establishes the non-existence of the past and future;
the second part determines the causes and conditions for establishing the system.
The preceding section has three parts:
first, it clarifies that the past and future do not exist;
second, it distinguishes the characteristics of the three periods of time.
The third section provides a detailed explanation in response to objections.
Within this, the first part clarifies its non-existence in the future,
while the latter part clarifies its non-existence in the past.
The commentary on this section is largely based on the *Jiaoshao*.
This refutes the theory that the past and future exist substantially (*dravyasat*).

In order to clarify the intrinsic nature (*svadharma*) of the three time periods, it first refutes that [theory] as a preliminary determination of causes, following the sixth stage of investigation (*vitarka-vicāra-bhūmi*) in the response.
This is not a definitive determination (*niścaya*), because it is a determination based on the dependent nature (*paratantra*) and so forth.
Why is this so? As stated in the subsequent objection.
This is a general challenge:
there is no sense in which that which lacks power can have the meaning of moving from one location to another location.
This refutes the first [position].
One should formulate the formal argument as follows:
Form in the future world must have a spatial location,
because it undergoes transformation.
Just as with present form,
furthermore, dharmas of the future cannot be transferred to the present world,
because they lack spatial location.
"Like the horns of a rabbit, etc.,
nor are they dharmas that have not yet arisen or have already arisen"—
this refutes the second [position].
It means that for a phenomenon that has not yet arisen,
death is necessarily non-existent,
because it has not arisen— just like space or like a rabbit’s horns.
"If that which arises by taking that as a condition were to arise as something different," and so forth—
this refutes the third [position].
That is to say, [the opponent claims] that a future dharma exists in its own right without perishing, and taking this as a condition, a distinct present dharma arises.
Since this dharma does not exist in the future, it would contradict your own tenet;
how then can you say that all dharmas inherently exist in the future? One should formulate the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) as follows:
This presently arising phenomenon does not exist as something seen in the future,
because it is devoid of arising,
just like the characteristics and functions of abiding, ceasing, and so forth.
Furthermore, regarding the statement that "in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), all phenomena lack activity (*kāritra*) and so forth," this refutes the fourth position of the proponent of activity.
Activity cannot be found apart from its substance (*svabhāva*).
Because the entity arises from something else;
just as the entity arises from its own self-nature. Even if one were to grant that they are different, [the fault remains].
The future must also possess functional activity (*karmatva*),
because it arises based upon its own substance (*svabhāva*),
just like present activity.
Furthermore, this karmic activity would then have to be originally non-existent and now newly produced;
while this would accord with the tenets of other schools,
it would contradict one's own school.
Because that school asserts that all phenomena exist in the future;
otherwise, one should likewise formulate the following formal argument (*pramāṇa*):
"The essential nature and characteristics of all things do not exist in the future."
Because it is not separated from karma,
just like present karma and so forth.
Furthermore, it contradicts the words of the Blessed One below.
To refute the existence of a substantial entity in the future,
one should formulate the following syllogism:
"The substantial entity of the future time must be eternal."
Because they exist as they originally were and exist as they are now,
like space and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "if, within a single characteristic, distinct portions of that characteristic were to obtain existence," etc.:
This refutes the fifth [position]: that the future aspect is incomplete while the present aspect is complete.
Regarding this, it says:
"If even a single part were to exist in the future while being incomplete," [it would follow that it is already present].
Why does this portion of perfection not exist in the future? One should formulate the following formal argument (*pramāṇa*):
"A portion of the characteristics of perfection that exists in the present will indeed exist in the future."
Because those [future phenomena] do not possess each individual part [as they exist now].
As the commentary on the *Pratītyasamutpādādivibhaṅganirdeśa-sūtra* states:
"The future dharmas are complete in their associated characteristics."
Because it is of one and the same substance as the present dharma,
it is like the characteristics of the present;
furthermore, the characteristics of the present would not be complete.
Because it is of the same substance as future dharmas,
it is like the characteristics of the future;
furthermore, regarding those [characteristics] that differ in aspect, which were previously non-existent and now exist, and so forth.

It is said:
"A portion of the future is incomplete; its association with [the present] is non-existent now and comes into being."
Because it is a portion of the characteristic.
It is like the characteristic of a portion of the present being complete.
Furthermore, as for that which is other than all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra), such as form (rūpa) and so forth, namely the future portion and so on.

This refutes the sixth [position]: that there exists a distinct future part (*bhāga*) separate from [the present], which is not material form (*rūpa*) and so forth; the present is likewise [not such a part]. Therefore, regarding the distinction between the three time periods, one should formulate the following formal argument (*pramāṇa*):
"That which you claim exists as a future part external to material form and so forth is certainly non-existent."
Because it cannot be apprehended by either direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) or inference (*anumāna*),
like a rabbit’s horn and so forth. Puguang says:
Apart from the formations such as form (*rūpa*), no other future portion can be found,
because it is not different in nature from form and the rest,
just like form itself.

Furthermore, regarding the claim that "the characteristic of the fruit does not exist in the future but exists only in the present," this characteristic of the fruit likewise is originally non-existent and now existent. How,
then, can it be said that everything exists in the future?
One should formulate the formal argument (*prayoga*) as follows:
At the time of the future world, there must be the characteristic of a fruit,
because it possesses the division of a temporal period.
As in the present world,
the "world-portion" refers to the future portion and so forth.
Within this, there are six teachers.
In the sixth *mūla* section mentioned above, there are seven reckonings,
which include two interpretations.
One says that those [sections] are the sixth and the seventh.

thus, there are six. Furthermore, another interpretation states:
That seventh [category] is precisely this sixth;
within this [sixth], there is no such thing as that sixth.
Next, the characteristics of the three periods of time are distinguished.
In the third section of the preceding *Maulī Bhūmi*,
it has already been explained that there are three kinds of the three periods of time (*tryadhvan*):
first, the three periods of time of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
Second, the three periods of time according to consciousness-only;
third, the three periods of time according to the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*). Regarding the three periods of time according to the characteristics of phenomena:
Furthermore, for example, when seeds in the present possess the meanings of "will exist" (*bhaviṣyat*) or "have existed" (*abhūta*), they are described as dharmas of the three times;
this is established regarding seeds in the same manner as the third [case] above,
which applies to manifest activity (*samudācāra*).
However, because the seeds are eternal, they are said not to be manifest activities.
Below, in the second [section], it states that there are three characteristics in the present:
the first is the characteristic of the past fruit.
Second is the characteristic of the future cause;
third is the present seed-nature, which is itself the characteristic of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).
Regarding the three time periods in the context of Consciousness-Only:
because the prior consciousness already possesses the objects of the past and those yet to come,
it is like ordinary beings perceiving objects of the past and future.
This object appears within the mind.
Because there is a function of false existence upon consciousness, images and marks arise that are non-different from consciousness; these appear as seeds of the three periods of time.
In reality, all these present phenomena rely upon seeds previously conditioned.
When this image arises conditioned by seeds,
it is called "representation-only" (vijñaptimātra) because it is false due to being representation-only.
In the third *mūla-sthāna* mentioned above,
it is stated that if the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is distracted spontaneously, it is termed "taking a present object as its domain," because its object is always present.
Question: Consciousness does not arise in isolation;
it arises based on an objective essence (ālambana-pratibimba) as its object.
If this [consciousness] were to arise by taking past or future objects as its conditions, [how would that be possible]?
Since it is recognized that there is no intrinsic nature,
how could objects arise?
It would be like atoms, space, and so forth.
It has teaching as its essence,
just as previously it was said to have seeds as its essence;
furthermore, what would constitute the essence of that which takes a rabbit's horn as its object?
All of these are merely seeking after names;
because they take names as their objective essence, images arise.
Therefore, it is "consciousness-only" (vijñaptimātra).
Regarding the non-arising of these things such as rabbit horns:
because there is no present cause for their arising,
just as in the past they were not the fruit of rabbit horns.
Therefore, the horns of a rabbit are not the same as the past.
That which possesses supernatural power across the three periods of time is precisely the supernormal knowledge of others' minds attained through meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
If ordinary persons and noble ones take the past as their object,
it appears as if present because the capacity for its arising remains; furthermore,
depending on whether the arising is strong or weak, the range of the perceived object may be broad or narrow.
This differs from the previous [position].
Alternatively, one might hold that the mind is not an object of direct perception (*pramāṇa*).
If one does not hold that it is perceived directly, then it is known through inference (*anumāna*).
Either one infers that a certain event will occur in the future by analogy with what has been seen in the past,
or one knows through inference by taking the present as a point of comparison for what previously existed.
If it concerns supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), these are all realized through understanding;
although they arise from mental faculties, they constitute realized concentration (*sākṣātkṛta-samādhi*).
Therefore, they are distinct from the former.
In the past, there must have been a fruit;
furthermore, in the present, it exists because it conforms to the cause that will exist in the future.
Since this discussion concerns only the cause, its [the fruit's] characteristics have already been set aside.
Because it does not take the fruit as its object, it is not said to exist in the present;
furthermore, this demonstrates that the past and future lack substantial reality,
and are designated as "past" only in relation to the present dharma.
Because it does not state that the fruit exists but rather states that its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) has already ceased,
it reveals that the characteristic of arising in the future likewise lacks substantiality.
It is said that the cause exists in the future.
Regarding the fact that there is the sense of a fruit yet to arise based on a present cause, this is established even for present phenomena.
It is clearly understood that while the substance of a past cause has already ceased, this cause once existed in relation to the present fruit; it does not exist as something currently present.
Thus, the past is established within the present life;
