The preceding section has three parts:
first, the formal determination of causes and conditions;
second, the clarification of the meaning of subduing and severing, as well as falling back or not falling back.
The seeds of the three knowledges (*trividyā*), the three feelings (*trivedanā*), and so forth, persist throughout successive states.
Regarding these, the first section first correctly establishes the causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*),
while the second section refutes the arguments of opponents.
The preceding section consists of an initial question, followed by an explanation, and concluding with a summary.

Regarding the statement: "The various material faculties (*rūpīndriya*), their bases (*āśraya*), and consciousness—these two briefly explained as being able to sustain the seeds of all phenomena (*sarvadharmabījādika*)," [it means as follows].
The "color of the auspicious clouds" refers to the five faculties, such as the eye-faculty and so forth.
The "basis of the faculties" corresponds to the faculties and their objects;
the "Great" [Reality] is unified with the faculties.
The mind is the second.
In this context, the mental factors (caitta) are not explained in detail;
it merely maintains the seeds of its own mental factors.
Regarding the statement "excluding the matter of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and so forth," this is discussed in terms of the internal sense-fields (*āyatana*).
It should be understood that external objects such as mountains and rivers are explained below in the section on the differentiation of the support of seeds.
"It is simply through internal consciousness and internal faculties that external seeds are produced.
Regarding this, Master Ji says:
"When the Tripiṭaka master speaks of the 'support of the faculties,' he refers to the sense-objects that sustain the faculties."
If that is so, why does the summary of all seeds below not mention the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*), and why does the subsequent passage state:
"It should be known that the remaining material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) are pursued solely by their own seeds"?
Since the meaning and the phrasing here appear contradictory, they are now explained.
"The support of the faculties" refers to the four great elements that serve as the basis for the faculties;
therefore, in the second section explaining the reason, it says:
If the material sense-faculties (*rūpīndriya*) and their own primary elements (*mahābhūta*) do not have the seeds of mind and mental factors (*cittacaitta*) following along with them,

and so forth— if that were so, why does the treatise state that "there are seeds of the material sense-faculties following the material sense-faculties," but does not say that "there are seeds of the material phenomena within the four great elements"?
The commentary states:
This is omitted here for brevity.
Furthermore, in the preceding general statement regarding the sense organs (*indriya*), their bases (*āśraya*), and the reasons therefor, it says "one's own four great elements" (*svamahābhūta*).
By clarifying that the sense faculties produced by the four great elements possess the seeds of all phenomena, the faculties have been explained here;
having explained the faculties, one has thereby explained the four great elements that produce them.
It should be understood from the treatise that the remaining material phenomena are followed solely by their own respective seeds.
This refers to the sense faculties and their objects,
not to the external material world.
For this reason, even among the mental factors (caitta-dharma), there must likewise exist their own seeds.
In this context, the term "consciousness" alone is used as a shorthand,
without further elaboration.
Furthermore, mental factors (caitta) differ from the sense organs and their objects.
For what reason? Because when the faculties and their objects—which support the mental factors—are absent, it might be possible for the mental factors to exist;
however, this is not the case.
How could they possibly exist when the sovereign [the mind] itself is absent?
Therefore, this does not serve as a precedent.
In this context, if there is a distinct form while the mind exists, where would the seeds reside?
Is it that every single form-factor (rūpa-dharma) and mental factor (citta-dharma) possesses all seeds?
This is not so; when there is mind, it resides in the mind, and when there is no mind, it resides in form.
If one hears that there is an intermediate state (antarābhava), then there are immeasurable seeds therein.
Furthermore, when one is born into the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), where do the seeds of form reside?
If it is argued that they reside in the mind,
then in what location do they reside when there is a mind in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*)?
If [the seed] exists within the mind,
why does it not exist within form?
Furthermore, below this follows the second rebuttal, in which the opponent is refuted for not establishing that the seed resides in either form or mind.
There are thus faults. First, it clarifies the fault that matter (*rūpa*) does not sustain seeds;
third, it clarifies the fault that the mind (*citta*) does not sustain seeds.
Regarding these treatises,

the subsequent statement that "all are based on the scriptural authority [of the Buddha] regarding the non-establishment of the ālayavijñāna" follows the Sautrāntika interpretation according to the gate of reasoning.
Next, the meaning of subduing, abandoning, falling back, and not falling back is explained.
First, the subduing by means of the worldly path is explained;
second, the abandoning by means of the supramundane path is explained.
The preceding section has two parts:
first, a brief summary, and second, a detailed exposition.
Regarding the defiled phenomena among all phenomena of the desire realm:
The seeds of afflictions and the seeds of other dharmas refer to the seeds of the wholesome and the neutral.
The extensive explanation of the three types of subduing through elimination is as follows:
first, subduing through distancing,
which refers to leaving the household life and receiving the precepts.
Being far removed from and severing the dust,
and abandoning and subduing the afflictions—
this is the wisdom attained in this life.
Second is subduing through weariness and aversion,
which refers to ethical discipline; it functions by means of the aspect of faults and disadvantages.
Contemplating the five objects of sensual desire as being capable of causing harm to oneself, harm to others, or harm to both,

is called the aspect of their disadvantages (*ādīnava-nimitta*). Alternatively, it refers to the abandonment of greed through the suppression [of desire] by means of the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) alone.
This [concentration] pertains to all three types of wisdom. Through the three forms of *śamatha*, afflictions are suppressed;
that is, the afflictions of the desire realm and the form realm are subdued.
Although the afflictions that have already been subdued and eliminated in the sphere of nothingness are also [included],
they are not said to be "separated from the formless" because the discussion is restricted to the desire realm.
The second section clarifies the permanent abandonment through the Noble Path.
Within this, first it clarifies the severance of the seeds of defilement at the time of entering the state with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa*);
second, it clarifies the impairment and suppression of the seeds of the wholesome and the neutral at the time of entering the state without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa*).
The statement that "according to the principle of non-arising, they are mutually not non-seeds" means that the contaminated path suppresses [the seeds] but does not sever them.

The metaphor of being damaged by fire represents the uncontaminated severance; at the moment of the diamond-like mind (*vajropama-citta*), all seeds of the three realms are forever destroyed, realizing the state of no-remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa*).
Regarding the fact that all seeds of the wholesome and neutral [dharmas] are suppressed at the time of entering the realm of nirvana without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa-dhātu*),
according to the *Vibhāṣā*, this refers to the moment when an Arhat of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) enters nirvana without remainder after having severed [the outflows].
Except for five or six moments of mind, all [other states] attain non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Regarding this passage, people have various interpretations.
First, this is based on the sequence of the eight minds of the desire realm:
first, the wholesome mind of preparatory effort (*prayoga-kuśala-citta*); second, the wholesome mind acquired at birth (*upapatti-lābhika-kuśala-citta*).
Third, unwholesome minds;
fourth, obscured minds;
fifth, constrained-and-arising minds.
Sixth, the mind of the six modes of deportment;
seventh, the mind of craftsmanship;
eighth, the mind of transformation.
At that time, one forms the intention to enter the state of nirvana without remainder;
this occurs either by excluding only the fifth consciousness, the mind of rebirth,
or by excluding only the sixth consciousness, the mind of deportment.
These two minds are the minds at the moment of death.
Apart from these two, all [other states] attain non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Alternatively, some explain it as follows:
When this Arhat wishes to enter nirvana without remainder,
he first abides in the power of the fourth limit-attaining concentration (prāntakoṭika-dhyāna),
excluding only the four dhyānas and the four applications of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna).
Excluding the fifth wholesome mind of the desire realm and the sixth non-obscured mind,
these are the minds at the time of death.
Apart from these six moments of mind, all others attain non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
What is the intention behind this?

It is because at that time, the practitioner enters the four dhyānas in reverse order from the "limiting concentration" (*prāntakoṭika-samādhi*), and only upon reaching the sixth moment of mind—whether it be wholesome or neutral—does he pass away.
This is not the case here;
for the subsequent text explains that one must enter the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) to extinguish the six consciousnesses,
and then pass away while abiding within the ālayavijñāna during that state of cessation.
Regarding the statement that "because the seeds of defiled phenomena have been extinguished, they can no longer produce their own kind of fruit," this means that at the time of the vajra-like mind,
the seeds of defilement and so forth are severed.
Causing virtuous seeds not to produce maturation and neutral seeds not to produce their own class of fruit—
this is called the fourth [type of] impairment and suppression.
As long as the seeds of defilement have not been severed,
they can assist the seeds of the wholesome and the indeterminate in obtaining their fruits;
[this ceases] by means of the permanent destruction of the seeds of defilement.
This means that the auxiliary factors are permanently destroyed;
thus, they are able to impair and suppress the seeds of the wholesome and neutral [states] so that they cannot produce their fruits.
Therefore, it is called "permanently destroying the auxiliaries and suppressing [the seeds]."
Regarding the statement "the fourth," there are two interpretations.
One says that being free from the defilements of the three realms is itself divided into three.
The fourth is called "permanently destroying the associates.
Second, it is said that while the previous [section] spoke of the three [practices] such as seclusion,
the present [section] speaks of permanently destroying the associates.
This is designated as the fourth.
According to the subsequent passage in the lower fascicle:
"Question: It has already been stated previously that the seeds of defiled phenomena (*kliṣṭa-dharma*) are suppressed and subdued."
What are the impairment and suppression of the seeds of wholesome dharmas?
The answer is: if various defiled dharmas that are contrary to the wholesome are constantly and intensely cultivated through habitual perfuming, this is the first impairment and suppression.
If one clings to false views and extensively practices such false views, as do the various non-Buddhists, this is the second impairment and suppression.
If one frequently practices only wrong views and slanders [the truth] such that one is like one who has severed the roots of goodness, this is the third form of impairment and suppression.
If one can permanently destroy the seeds of defiled phenomena,
it is as previously explained.
This is the fourth [point of] subduing through impairment.
Below this, the third section clarifies that the seeds follow along with all states, such as the three types of sensation;
first, they follow the mind associated with the phenomena of the three sensations.
Next, it conforms to the mind of the three natures;
next, it conforms to the mind of the stage of training;
next, it conforms to the stage beyond training.
Even when a learner gives rise to an untainted mind, it is still pursued by the seeds of affliction.
From here on, the second section establishes the conditions of dependent origination based on the gateway of ultimate truth.
This is divided into two parts:
first, concluding the preceding section and establishing the causal conditions for what follows;
second, reconciling divergent explanations found in the sutras.
It should be understood that when it is said "at that time, because of abandoning and falling back," "falling back" refers to falling back from what has been suppressed and abandoned;
this is also "falling back from abiding."
Due to falling back from a higher state,
one may fail to manifest and abide in an impure meditative concentration;
this is called "abiding in decline."
This refers to falling back from what has been practiced.
Tai states that those beyond training (aśaikṣas) may fall back from the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti);
however, this does not accord with the present text.
